items.body: There are places that become so closely associated with geopolitics that it is easy to forget they are still inhabited landscapes, with their own geology, ecosystems and daily rhythms. Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran, is one such place. On Aerial Roots, Mo Farzaneh turns his attention to the island itself, drawing on field recordings made across its coastlines, villages, mountains and Hara mangrove forests. Wind, birds, water and traces of human activity are woven into electronics that grow directly from the environments he encountered. As Farzaneh explains in our interview, repeated visits taught him to recognise structures already present in the soundscape: changes in density across day and night, shifting winds and, above all, the tides, whose cycles repeat without ever producing exactly the same configuration. “Tabl” opens with wind carrying faint evidence of human presence through crackling environmental noise and birdsong, while sweeping shifts in pitch from a rising and falling wail give the piece a ghostly atmosphere. “Doulab” becomes more languid, bringing water and birds into sharper focus as an incantatory, revolving figure recalls the doulab, the traditional water wheel from which the piece takes its name. Circularity becomes still more pronounced on “Distant Memories”, where the movement of waves is translated into electronic material. Farzaneh describes the sea as an image of memory: each wave replaces the previous one while the underlying rhythm persists. The thirteen-minute “Aerial Roots” pushes this exchange further, playing with resonance until the natural ecosystem begins to resemble a negative imprint of its synthesised counterpart; towards the end, the environmental sounds gradually reclaim the foreground. “Sandstone Canyon”, meanwhile, introduces sharper sonic peaks and greater dynamic variation. The title catches something essential about Farzaneh’s method. Roots normally imply attachment to a particular ground; these roots have become airborne. His field recordings retain evidence of actual places and events, while percussive elements carry traces of particular practices, yet both can be detached, transformed and recomposed. Farzaneh noticed how Qeshm’s acoustic environment changes near piers and other centres of human activity, where species audible in quieter areas disappear beneath the noise of boats, while human sounds themselves can become strangely disembodied. Having moved to Qeshm after years in Tehran, he approaches the island as a stranger learning how to listen, deliberately resisting the temptation to interpret the lives he encounters. The album never turns these concerns into an environmental manifesto. Instead, vulnerability is embedded in its shifting cycles, where repetition always contains small changes and nothing remains sonically fixed. As Farzaneh writes of the Hara mangroves, this is “an ecosystem whose cycles have repeated here for thousands of years, now seeming more fragile than ever.” photo by Mo Farzaneh To find out more about the location and the recording process we asked Mo Farzaneh a few questions. Aerial Roots grew out of recordings made across Qeshm Island, from the Hara mangrove forests and coastline to mountains and villages, and you describe field recording less as collecting material than as a way of “spending time with a place”. Listening to the album, birds, water, wind and other environmental sounds often seem to determine the music’s rhythm and structure rather than simply provide atmosphere. How much did the environments themselves teach you how to compose? Were there moments when you found yourself following patterns already present in water, birdsong or wind rather than imposing a musical structure upon them? Yes, a lot. At the beginning of my field recording work, it was mostly the sound events themselves that caught my attention. But gradually I stopped thinking only about collecting raw material. I kept going back to the same places at different times, and I started noticing how the sound environment changed with the weather or with human activity. Those repeated visits made the place itself show me its rhythms and patterns. The way the density of sound shifted throughout the day and night was already a kind of musical structure. I just listened to it and tried to keep that structure in the composition. The electronic parts are basically my emotional and inner response to those patterns more like a conversation between the sounds of the place and my own reaction as someone who was there listening. I should also say that after years of living in Tehran, moving to Qeshm felt completely different. The unfamiliarity of that listening environment changed the way I hear things, and that shift still feels valuable to me. photo by Mo Farzaneh Your photographs repeatedly move between very large landscapes and extremely close observations of surfaces: eroded rock, cracked earth, tidal patterns in sand, mangrove roots, weathered walls. There is something similar in the music, where a recognisable environment can suddenly seem to dissolve into microscopic textures, drones and electronic detail. When you were photographing, recording and composing on Qeshm, did these different ways of looking and listening begin to influence one another? And do you see the photographs as documentation of the places behind Aerial Roots, or as another part of the same artistic work? Yes, I had already started photographing on the island before I began recording sound. Looking through the camera helped the direction of the project become clearer. Gradually I noticed that photography was affecting the sound sources I chose, and the other way around working on the sounds pushed me to take more photos, and more varied ones. Sometimes looking at a place through the camera while listening to it at the same time also changed how I structured the pieces or processed the sounds. Making this album and connecting with the place through these different ways made me want to share the other things I had collected too. That’s why I see the photographs as part of the work itself, not just documentation. They’re both telling the same experience, just from different angles. photo by Mo Farzaneh In your notes on the Hara mangroves, you describe an extraordinarily organised daily sound cycle: birds and other creatures gradually becoming more active, frogs joining the soundscape, crickets occupying the night, and the first bird at dawn effectively marking another transition. You also describe the ecosystem as having repeated these cycles for thousands of years while now appearing “more fragile than ever”. There is a comparable tension in Aerial Roots between repetition and constant small change. Did those ecological cycles provide a model for the album’s sense of musical time, and how consciously did the environmental vulnerability of Qeshm enter the work? Yes, but it was more a matter of gradually becoming aware of it. Because I was recording in the forest at different times of day and night, I started paying closer attention to how the environment was changing. I slowly noticed a recurring cycle things would repeat, but they were always slightly different. Even now, whenever I go back to those recordings, I hear something new. The changes weren’t just about day and night. The tides played a big role too. The activity of the creatures in the forest seemed to move with the tide, constantly shifting the sound. Places that at first seemed completely still were actually changing all the time. The wind direction could change several times in a day, the light would move across the water, and a bird I heard from one direction in the morning might come from somewhere else in the afternoon. Even something as repetitive as the daily cycle of the forest took on a slightly different shape each time. This gave me a strong sense of the tension between stability and constant small change a pattern that repeats without ever being exactly the same. That quality became something I paid attention to while working on the album. I tried to keep a similar feeling in the structure of the pieces. I was also constantly aware of how vulnerable Qeshm’s natural environment is in the face of human presence. The more I moved around the island, the clearer this became. Many of the quieter places, simply because they were further from busier areas, had a completely different sonic character. There were bird sounds you simply don’t hear near the piers, where the noise and activity of boats made the environment very different. That contrast stayed with me throughout the process. photo by Mo Farzaneh Memory seems to occupy an important place in Aerial Roots, most explicitly in the title “Distant Memories.” Field recording might initially appear to be an act of preservation — fixing a particular place and moment in time — yet your electronic processing allows those recordings to move away from their original form and acquire new associations. How do you understand the relationship between remembering and transforming in your work? Are you interested in preserving something of Qeshm as you experienced it, or in allowing those memories to change and acquire a new life through composition? Being part of this process made me think more about my relationship with places. No recording can fully represent a place. It can only capture one layer of the experience of being there tied to that specific day and time. What remains is a kind of sonic memory, and that memory keeps changing. When I enter an unfamiliar place, I usually slow down and listen before trying to understand what I’m hearing. Sound leaves more room for imagination than a fixed visual image. I start to experience the space less as something solid and more as something alive and constantly shifting. Listening to something unstable and fleeting feels closely connected to memory for me. A sound happens, disappears, and becomes part of what I remember. When I return to it later, I’m not necessarily hearing the same thing anymore. The recording is still there, but my relationship to it has changed. This became especially clear while working on “Distant Memories.” I took the continuous sound of the sea and worked with it in a way that keeps the underlying rhythm of the waves, but never lets any single wave stay for long. As one wave arrives, it gradually replaces the previous one, and then it too fades as the next one takes its place. In a way, the piece became an image of how memory works for me: something arrives, stays for a moment, and is slowly replaced. We don’t necessarily lose the memory completely, but its original form becomes more distant each time. The sea felt like a continuous memory the rhythm remains, but the individual waves are always temporary. That’s probably what interested me about it in the first place. photo by Mo Farzaneh Qeshm is not only an extraordinary natural environment but an island with a remarkably layered human history: inhabited since prehistoric times, shaped by successive empires and occupations, and for centuries positioned along maritime routes connecting Iran with India, China and East Africa. Your notes, however, approach the island at a much more intimate scale — people talking between houses, fishermen working on their nets, a goatherd calling in the morning, children cycling through a village, or someone inviting you into their home and offering you dates. What is your own personal relationship with Qeshm, and how much did you want Aerial Roots to engage not only with its landscapes and ecosystems but with the lives, histories and cultural memory of the people who inhabit them? My personal relationship with Qeshm is that of a stranger who’s gradually getting to know a place. Maybe that distance is why things that feel ordinary and everyday to the people who live there still feel fresh and worth noticing to me. That sense of newness is what made me want to listen to them and record them. As I spent time going around different villages and parts of the island, I started to sense something of the island’s history and collective memory in the rhythms of everyday life, rather than in its buildings or official stories. The way people adapt to the climate and their environment, and the kind of resilience in how they live, really stood out. The closer I listened, the harder it became to draw a clear line between the natural and human soundscapes of the island. For me, people’s lives were just as much a part of Qeshm’s soundscape as the mangroves or the sea. Since I was a stranger myself, still learning how to listen to this place and the people in it, I preferred not to explain or interpret their lives. I just let their presence stay part of my experience of the island. Maybe that’s why what I saw and heard found its way more into the sounds I chose and the overall atmosphere of the album than into talking about it directly. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以伊朗霍尔木兹海峡格什姆岛的实地录音为核心素材，将海岸线、村庄、山地与红树林中的风声、水声、鸟鸣与人类活动痕迹编织进电子声响之中。录音并非简单叠加，而是经过深度转化：海浪的周期性运动被翻译为电子材料，水流回旋呼应传统水车的结构，不同曲目分别聚焦于潮汐、记忆、岩石峡谷等主题。十三分钟的同名曲中，自然声音与合成器相互置换，形成负像般的共振关系。整体制作强调循环中的微小变化与不可重复的声学配置，不诉诸环保宣言，而是以脆弱性与流动感呈现一个充满地缘政治色彩却仍鲜活可感的岛屿生态。

items.body:
The previous Ezz-thetics column reflected the near-simultaneous appearance of three works of individual brilliance, solo recordings by Liz Allbee, Hannah Marshall, and John Butcher. In the months since, three mid-size, improvisation-rich ensembles, drawing inspiration from more or less explicit environmental themes have appeared, with varying degrees of composition and improvisation, led by musicians of comparable vision: Magda Mayas, Pascal Niggenkemper, and Marta Warelis.

Each is characterized by different degrees of copyright participation, signalling contrasting relations of composition and improvisation. Magda Mayas’ Filamental’s Murmur, evidently as collective as a murmuration of starlings, is copyrighted in the names of all eight musicians. Pascal Niggenkemper’s d’une rive a l’autre is largely copyrighted to the composer/bassist, 11 of the 17 tracks, with six tracks credited to improvised duets from the eight instrumentalists of the Ensemble Tuvalu. Marta Warelis’s Still Life with Lemons is largely credited to the leader/composer. All recently released, the three come from a specific moment in time, the autumn of 2024: Murmur was recorded in Berlin in September; Still Life with Lemons in Amsterdam in October; d’une rive a l’autre in Berlin in November.

Magda Mayas’ Filamental’s Murmur (Relative Pitch) is an octet with a strong emphasis on strings in its make-up; as well as the leader’s piano, there are two harpists, Zeena Parkins and Rhodri Davies, pretty much covering the terrain of free improvising harpists; two cellists, Aimée Theriot-Ramos and Anthea Caddy; two reeds, alto saxophonist Christine Abdelnour and clarinetist Michael Thieke, and violinist Angharad Davies. Murmur is a singular piece, almost 38 minutes long.

There are few spectacles as emblematic of collective mind as a murmuration of starlings, thousands of birds joined in extraordinary aerobatic maneuvers that mock the reckless waste, noise, and danger of fighter jet ballets. Part of the special genius of Magda Mayas’ Filamental is that it never sounds anything like what one might expect from its string-heavy personnel. Everything is sublimated into quiet percussive events, a music that suggests the sublime piety of chance events in nature, like a light rain on large leaves. Hence, Mayas’ description of the work:

I am fascinated by the coordination and elegance of a flock of birds flying, forming beautiful murmurations, constantly changing, seemingly without effort. This communal act provides protection through the sheer number of birds and their changing position; it is an exchange of information amongst them, and it has a clear collective ending when the flock decides to fly back to the ground.

In Murmur, I want to explore how a large ensemble can make use of these instincts of communal movement, coordination, shape shifting and, eventually, potential simultaneous endings through distinct decisions around material and structure but also shared memories of events that were created together.

The doubling of instruments will lend a certain anonymity to the music, furthered by the frequency of isolated percussive details, whether a sustained note from Abdenour suggests a bowed string instrument, or cellos and/or violin are used for a maze of quarter tones. It’s the very nature of the murmuration that will define this collective composition, hive mind or flock consciousness, yes, some overriding shared awareness, existence, and impulse. With no dedicated percussionist present (depending on how you might classify the piano), this is frequently percussion music of the highest order, struck strings on piano and string instruments create a bevy of string-drum plosives. The collective act itself is essentially harmonious in its nature, the special transparency of string harmonics creating a sonic window that opens onto the Cagean silence of the entire ensemble. The cumulative experience is of an interior soundscape in art channeled through the piano and taking place both in the octet and in the listener. A rare and beautiful sonic act.

Pascal Niggenkemper’s Ensemble Tuvalu’s d’une rive a l’autre (Subran 07) is inspired by Tuvalu, the Polynesian archipelago that is currently set to disappear below the Pacific’s waves in a few decades, a paradisical world doomed by climate change. As with Mayas’ Murmur, the bassist/composer’s ensemble is an octet, made up of instrumental pairings: Ben LaMar Gay’s cornet with Louis Lorain’s trumpet; Mona Matbou Riahi’s clarinet with Joachim Badenhorst’s; Tizia Zimmermann’s accordion with that of Artemis Vavatsika’s; Niggenkemper’s double bass paired, less precisely, with Elisabeth Coudoux’s cello. Each of the musicians will also have a vocal role, singing, chanting, or reciting, and Jaumes Privat will appear near the end of the work for an extended spoken word passage.

In her expansive liner note, Julia Neupert, cites the composer’s overarching concerns here:

Niggenkemper is interested in how differently people are shaped – culturally, socially, emotionally – not only in musical terms. He is concerned with broadening perspectives, recognizing other points of view, and collective thinking and creation. In this way, the project also reflects a central cultural value of Tuvaluan society: “Kaitasi” – the principle of always shaping one’s own life in connection with the community. An idea that could hardly be more relevant in our time.

d’une rive a l’autre is a work of daunting complexity. In a “live” staging, drums and metal discs are center stage; a series of 16 sound curtains of plastic and metal with exciter resonators activated by foot pedals surround the stage. All the musicians sing and speak traditional Tuvaluan songs and poems as well as singing freely adapted poems drawn from multiple languages. It comes as both a CD and a DVD. The CD was recorded over four days in the Südwestrundfunk Baden-Baden studio. It has 17 tracks and represents something like the totality of the audio work. The DVD was recorded with an audience in the Tollhaus Karlsruhe a day later. It has 12 tracks, is significantly shorter, sacrifices the instrumental duets, but is enriched by sheer theatrical intensity. Either way, it’s stellar work, with Niggenkemper’s insistence on a humane art reflecting both human potential and the necessity of engaging our collective condition with work of special power. The multiple demands that he places on his musicians are answered with stunning results in the additional tracks on the studio recordings, reflecting the brief individual duets among the matched instruments.

The DVD performance was also presented on the Free Jazz Blog at the time of its release, and it remains available online. It’s an immediate introduction to the work’s combination of visceral emotional power and often luminous instrumental textures:

https://www.freejazzblog.org/2025/03/pascal-niggenkempers-tuvalu-ensemble.html

Marta Warelis’s Still Life with Lemons (Relative Pitch) may be less immediately shaped by environmental concerns than the preceding, but lyric ideas of landscape and the impress of environment still figure in her compositions, from “Birds” to “The Sky Blushes Sunset” to “Ashes to Sea.” The group is a multi-national sextet, with the Polish pianist/synthesist Warelis joined by Hollander Ab Baars, clarinet, tenor saxophone; Canadian Karen Ng, clarinet, alto saxophone; Norwegian Ingebrigt Håker Flaten, double bass; and Americans Ben LaMar Gay, trumpet and electronics and Frank Rosaly drums and gongs. That might suggest a forceful, wind-driven ensemble, but the emphasis is reflective, intimate, sometimes pensive, often witty. Thin instrumental textures predominate, sometimes with different instruments’ sounds penetrating one another, even creating beat patterns as pitches approach one another.

The opening “Birds” begins with an extended solo piano passage immediately emphasizing a certain intimacy. It will persist as the horns enter, with significant dissonance, in a slow interweaving of instrumental voices, ultimately matching the longing of the winds’ theme against the chaotic rush of Warelis and the rhythm section. “There to the Bridge,” an Albanian folk song, receives a plaintively nostalgic performance with Gay setting the mood before the two clarinetists carry the mournful theme to its furthest reaches. The band possesses genuine wit, as apparent in “Alternate Endings,” continuously propelled by Warelis and Håker Flaten’s broken rhythms, effectively extended by the flaring tone of Gay’s trumpet and the dense squawking supplied by Baars’ tenor saxophone. “Intermittent Web of Sorts” proceeds from the initially hesitant patterns of Håker Flaten and Rosaly before Warelis and Gay introduce the theme, textures gradually accumulating. It ultimately reaches an accumulation of sustained winds and electronics, pitches sliding in and out of beat patterns, a high point in the music’s special interconnectedness.
items._cn_summary: 本文聚焦近期三支中型即兴乐团的专辑，分别由Magda Mayas、Pascal Niggenkemper和Marta Warelis领衔。文章以椋鸟群飞（murmuration）为隐喻切入，详述Mayas领衔的八重奏Filamental如何通过钢琴、两把竖琴、两把大提琴、单簧管与中音萨克斯及小提琴的弦乐主导编制，将所有声音转化为安静的打击式事件，仿佛自然中的偶然诗意——大叶片上的细雨。文中引用Mayas本人对群鸟协调、集体运动与同步收束的描述，揭示作品试图探索大型团体如何借助共享结构记忆实现即兴中的集体决策。Niggenkemper的d'une rive a l'autre以作曲家署名为主，辅以六首即兴二重奏；Warelis的Still Life with Lemons则以领导者署名居多。三张专辑均来自2024年秋冬的柏林与阿姆斯特丹录音，呈现出当代欧洲实验即兴场景对环境意象与集体即兴关系的多元探索。

items.body:
This New World CD is by my count the fourth or fifth edition in half a century of a record that should never go out of print. Julius Hemphill released it on LP soon after its 1972 recording on his Mbari label. (Its name is writ large on the original cover; his own name did not appear. New World adds it to the facsimile cover.) He distributed it himself, and not many copies circulated. The album came out to a larger world with the 1977 version in Arista/Freedom’s new music series, with a new and striking cubistic photo-montage cover by Dennis Pohl, and liner notes by Robert Palmer which told us a bit about the West African Dogon people, and about Fort Worth–reared St. Louis–seasoned Hemphill. Curiously Palmer never IDs the backbones of Hemphill’s backbeat, cellist Abdul Wadud and ex-Paul Butterfield, ex-Art Ensemble of Chicago drummer Philip Wilson. (He did mention Julius’ right hand, trumpeter Baikida Carroll.) Advance word of a sort had come the previous year, with the release of Hemphill’s Arista/Freedom Coon Bid’ness, mostly recorded in 1975. It included “The Hard Blues” left over from the 1972 session, a tune which added Hamiet Bluiett’s bari to the core tet. A 2011 (pricey) limited edition CD miniaturizing the Pohl/Palmer package was produced by International Phonograph’s late Jonathan Horwich, who remastered the program from the original tapes, sensibly tacking on “The Hard Blues” as a bonus track. So does the New World version, which also sports new notes by Hemphill colleague/scholar/archivist Marty Ehrlich. The sound has been newly refurbished by Paul Zinman, cleaning up the raggedy/degraded tape ending of “Rites.” (I haven’t seen it, but there’s also a new Superior Viaduct LP edition of the original program/artwork, with notes by John Corbett.)

Wadud’s cello voice is prominent on Coon Bid’ness’ choogling “Skin 1” and “Skin 2,” but even with that album to whet a new Hemphill fan’s appetite, Abdul’s entrance at the top of Dogon’s 15-minute opening/title track was a stunner. First time I heard it, 49 years ago, I fell in love with the album before Julius had sounded a note: Wadud’s grinding one-bar bowed-dyads ostinato turned cello into a big Delta blues guitar. Wadud wasn’t the first jazz cello player by a long shot, though earlier ones mostly treated it like a baby bass. Other improvising cellists cropped up in the 1970s – Diedre Murray, David Eyges, Tristan Honsinger, Tom Cora, Ernst Reijseger ... – with many more soon to come, but nobody brought earthy sensibility and downhome funk to intonation and frictive bowing like Wadud. “Dogon”’s grinder riff nestled in the cracks in Philip Wilson’s sparse 11/16 drums and cymbal tattoo (a 4+4+3 he found tricky to master and held onto, tight, for most of it). And then come the horns, alto and trumpet melded in unison, and occasional blue minor harmony, phrasing like a single entity – the yoked horns of World Saxophone Quartet coming. (WSQ was already active when Arista/Freedom’s Dogon came out.) That melody is a series of bluesy aphoristic phrases that build on what’s already unfolded, then atomizes into a series of exclamatory single notes. The overall structure mirrors that odd-meter bar: the main melody’s sections are 19, 11 and 13 bars long.) In practice the melody seems capable of infinite development, while leaving space for cello and drums to speak through. (The cello part’s built-in variations may outline the harmony, arco or pizz.) And then comes Hemphill’s alto solo over vamping. Ornette’s North Texas holler is somewhere in the distance behind it, but Julius’s tone is dryer and harsher, his blues-infused intonation more sour and pitiless, his wildly scouring line informed by the written material: it’s all of a piece. He boils over and keeps boiling. (Baikida eases into his spot – won’t compete with that.) The blues gets dehydrated and reconstituted.

“Dogon A.D.” is all slow build; swifter “Rites” plunges right into the twisty melody; we’re in the thick of action from the opening seconds, fast but with no fixed tempo, its recurring hook (and opening) a couldn’t-be-simpler drop of a whole step. Thick is right: three-part harmony with cello as third horn, or sometimes as droning tambura. (If Ornette’s in there, it’s the roiling Crisis.) Baikida is especially effective darting behind Julius, blowing bugler’s commentary, reinforcing but never upstaging the boss’ alto. “Rites” is all coiled energy; when it flags, return to the head for a quick exit. For still more contrast, there’s the slowly unwinding “The Painter” for Hemphill’s bucolic sung-multiphonics flute (refreshingly un-Rahsaan-like), its melody both wide-ranging and sing-song catchy. Timing and articulation can be tricky – it’s not a line a part-time flutist writes for an easy layup. Wadud strums or picks rhythm; Wilson rustles; Carroll is as ever the loyal supporter, nimbly selfless, has chops to burn but keeps them in check. It’s the composer’s show, even without Hemphill’s name on the original cover.

And then “The Hard Blues” with its stompy riffy head, looking directly ahead to (and featuring half of) WSQ, but also – with its achingly-slow-to-quick tempos and dense-to-lean textures, suite-like variety and scored interludes – to Henry Threadgill’s 1980s Sextett. Whatever else he did, Julius Hemphill (like other members of St. Louis’s BAG co-op) brought convincing funk to new acoustic jazz, and reaffirmed the blues as eternal wellspring. Timeless tunes, an original group sound, liberatory cello – their appeal does not wear thin. Ehrlich’s notes describe in detail a private video of an earlier performance of the “Dogon A.D.” suite including a first unrecorded movement. The quartet was Hemphill, Carroll, Wilson and pre-Wadud pianist John Hicks, on vibes, playing what I’ve always thought of as the idiosyncratic ‘cello part.’ I imagine this performance as something from an alternate universe, one where Hemphill never performed at Oberlin College in 1970, and never met and jammed with the cellist known to classical audiences as Ronald DeVaughn, and that earthy blue arco scrape never got to shake us to the core.

Ideally Dogon A.D. and Coon Bid’ness should be reissued together, a definitive picture of Hemphill’s (and Wadud’s) music in early bloom. Rights to both are currently held by Germany’s DA Music. But both together are just too long to fit on a single CD. (With thanks to Marty Ehrlich for fielding various questions.)

items.body: (Colin Currie Group perform Steve Reich’s Quartet) Steve Reich’s ninetieth anniversary year would not be complete without a world premiere. Or two, as was the case in this evening’s all-Reich concert at Usher Hall, Edinburgh. There again, a Reich premiere would not be complete without the Colin Curry Group either, with Quartet (also on the programme) and Traveler’s Prayer previous co-commissions for Currie’s group. Forming part of this year’s Edinburgh International Festival, these two new compositions – Two Pianos and the stirring, spectacular In All Your Ways – appeared in either half of the program. More on that later. The evening began with Clapping Music, probably Reich’s most performed piece. Currie performed the piece on several occasions with Reich himself and recently told me that the experience was, in his words: ‘Completely surreal, yet not at all nerve-wrecking. Reich was a great person to take to the stage with, and I miss that interaction. I’m so glad I had that opportunity to perform with him.’ Certainly, fellow percussionist Owen Gunnell acquitted himself to the task at the Usher Hall’s reverberant acoustics, the duet executing the piece’s gradually shifting patterns with relaxed and consummate ease. This was followed by the first of two premieres. Two Pianos was originally composed by Reich in 2020, but for various reasons (the Pandemic amongst them) was held back until this year. Chorale-like in scope, the stately, slow-moving four-minute work revolved around a series of imposing harmonic pillars whose true significance was only completely revealed during a full and final statement at the end. Thereafter, the program took an upturn in energy and pace. The opening movement of the Radiohead-inspired Radio Rewrite for ensemble gained much from the way in which Curry – now conducting – managed to bind together its complex movable parts, his ensemble always alert to the music’s sudden shifts and tricky corners. The performance also managed to set the music’s propulsive qualities very effectively against more plangent moments heard during the second and fourth sections, while the closing movement rocked and rolled with more swagger and conviction than the Bon Jovi concert taking place down the road at the Murrayfield Stadium the same evening. Double Sextet provided a virtuosic end to the first half, with the first movement surging out of the blocks like a tearaway train and the third movement forever straining at the leash. The second half began much as the first had ended, this time with Quartet, pianists Philip Moore and Siwan Rhys and percussionists Currie and Gunnell locked tightly together throughout, sculpting the music’s peaks and troughs with power, accuracy, and precision. And so, to the evening’s highlight: Reich’s new work In All Your Ways. Scored for three sets of quartets (comprising woodwinds, percussion and strings), plus two pianos, the title is taken from Proverbs 3:6: ‘In all your ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct your paths.’ About as far removed from the composer’s recent Traveler’s Prayer as one could imagine, In All Your Ways was a revelation: Reich rethought and rewrought. Teeming with cascades of rising and falling lines that followed each other with almost breathless virtuosity and abandon, In All your Ways was far more linear in scope than what we have come to expect from this composer. Reich will often combine lines and layers vertically rather than horizontally. Once a rhythmic pattern and harmonic foundation is stated, he will then present and develop the material by gradually introducing interlocking lines and close canons above them. Reich’s musical conception is often therefore ‘simultaneous’ rather than ‘successive’, with patterns appearing as subdivisions of the beat. In All Your Ways appears to turn that idea on its head. These rhythmic subdivisions result in ever-shifting and ever-changing kaleidoscopic colours – a dizzying sequence of melodic spirals. Alongside these uplifting passages, a middle section provided a tender lyrical moment that seemed to draw on the melodic character of Reich’s opera The Cave. The work also ended with a beautiful moment where time appeared to stand still. Reich has noted that In All Your Ways is based on four rhythmic sections (sixteenths, eighths, quarters, triplets) alongside four harmonic areas, but the impression was of something more fluid, integrated, and organic. One cannot draw too many conclusions from one performance, of course, but In All Your Ways is a powerhouse of a piece that ranks alongside some of the composer’s other late masterpieces, such as Runner and Reich/Richter. If you missed the premiere, Colin Currie Group will also be performing In All Your Ways at the Concertgebouw, Amsterdam on September 19; Barbican, London on October 28; Philharmonie, Paris on November 22; and Großer Saal, Hamburg on December 4; with Canadian and US premieres featuring Soundstreams Canada and Ensemble Signal, Bang on a Can All-Stars and Brad Lubman, taking place on October 6 & 22 respectively. Not to be missed. The post Colin Currie Group Plays Steve Reich (Edinburgh International Festival, 28 August 2026) appeared first on Sequenza21.

items._cn_summary: 文章记录了Colin Currie Group在爱丁堡国际艺术节上演奏Steve Reich作品的整场音乐会。曲目涵盖Reich经典之作如拍手音乐、双六重奏与四重奏，并包含两首世界首演：2020年创作的双钢琴作品以及为三组四重奏和两架钢琴而作的全新力作In All Your Ways。乐评详尽描述了每首作品的演绎细节：拍手音乐在混响空间中的从容对位、Radio Rewrite中指挥对复杂节奏脉络的把控、双六重奏爆发般的张力，以及四重奏中钢琴与打击乐声部间精准的咬合。In All Your Ways的编制与宗教文本标题暗示了Reich晚期对深层次结构与精神维度的探索。整体演出在能量递进与情绪起伏的编排上展现了极高的艺术水准，凸显Reich九秩之年仍在持续拓展其极简主义语言的可能性。

items.body: The “distractions” of Greg Kelley’s trumpet and Yoona Kim’s ajaeng on this new album for Relative Pitch are hardly simple diversions for the listener, as one often thinks about the term. Actually, I find the music on this lovely duet recording to be at various times quieting, disruptive, disturbing, and even a challenge. Listeners familiar with Greg Kelley’s recorded output will not be shocked by what they hear, and at times this album reminds me a great deal of the trumpet player’s provocative, whisper-improvising duo Nmperign. Actually, the other half of that duo, Bhob Rainey, mixed and mastered Distractions . Kelley performs wonderfully and utilizes a reticence that nearly always prevents him from easily erupting into high energy bursts. His patience and discipline are admirable. The unexplored story here, however, is ajaeng player Yoona Kim. I was not familiar with Kim’s instrument of choice, and this reality is part of what first drew me to this recording. An ajaeng is a Korean zither-like instrument–think a bendier, more temperamental cello laid on its back. It can be plucked, but is often bowed with a stick or a more standard Western bow of horsehair. Kim is a polymath of musical styles and performs at least seven distinct genres, according to her website. Free improvisation and jazz are two of these, as are contemporary and traditional Korean music. The others are more surprising: Delta Blues, Klezmer, and Appalachian Old-Time Music. Despite an extensive set of online live performances, Kim is still relatively young and has only three recordings as a leader to her name. Distractions is one of these, and the other two, Deltat Dokkaebi and Modern Gagok, are all but impossible to find. A strong outing with pianist Anthony Coleman can be viewed here . This dazzling performance has a mere 25 views and 2 likes as of this writing. Free Jazz Blog readers, you know what to do. With all this being said, Yoona Kim is particularly challenging to define, though she has performed in some of the revered free jazz spaces (The Stone, for a week-long residence in July of 2026) and studied or played with many names readers of the FJC are quite familiar with: Tom Rainey, Chris Corsano, Joe Morris, and Linda May Han Oh. And of course, Greg Kelley. Distractions for Trumpet and Ajaeng is a wonderful album, full of quiet restraint and unsettling surprises. While the opening track, “Display,” starts with insistent blowing and bending, the first minute and a half is about as busy as the album gets. Kim bows and pulls the strings of her ajaeng while Greg Kelley flutters a raspy, metallic horn down into registers so low and frequencies so wobbly I had to stop the music to see if something was wrong with my speakers. The aesthetic largely, however, is quiet. To be more precise, silence that alternates with tiny eruptions of activity. Listen to the second track, the lovely “Dispute,” for this as Yoona Kim rips and bows urgently just before the one minute mark, at which point the recording falls into total silence. When the musicians return, Greg Kelley is more active and works his way into an exploration of one wavering note. This interplay builds as the two play an eerie high-harmony fit for hungry ghosts that largely bends and vibrates as it squeals and scrapes. While the dynamics never really reach the loudest of volumes, all of this silence makes certain mid-level insertions of noise jarring. For example, on my favorite piece on the album, the closer “Disappear,” Kelley forces air through his horn with such subtle power, and balances a series of soft notes so sinister, that my dog ran out of the room when I first played it. This, of course, is the power of understatement, and the album as a whole serves as a wonderful reminder that so often in music, as in our day-to-day laboring, what produces joy or excitement, as well as heaviness, sorrow, or surprise is how the moments fall together. Distractions is a delight of quiet echoes and disquieting interruptions that is well worth the listen. Distractions for Trumpet & Ajaeng by Greg Kelley and Yoona Kim Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由小号手Greg Kelley与韩国牙筝演奏家Yoona Kim合作，呈现为一场跨文化即兴对话。Kelley以极度克制的呼吸与低频颤音著称，声音金属感强且常游走于可听性边缘；Kim的牙筝则提供丰富纹理——既可拨弦也可弓弦，声音介于大提琴与伽倻琴之间，带有明显的东亚传统色彩。两人构建的审美以静默为主，在长时间的留白中偶尔爆发短促的能量，形成不安而内省的氛围。专辑由独立小厂牌Relative Pitch发行，Bhob Rainey负责混音。Kim的跨文化背景——涵盖自由即兴、传统韩国音乐、Delta Blues、克莱兹默与阿巴拉契亚民间音乐——使此次合作成为真正意义上的东西方实验融合，展现了器乐即兴的广阔可能性。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Horizons expand as if opening a door that leads neither to the past nor the future, though elements of both are present; this defines the character of Papangu, a Brazilian quintet that draws on numerous influences yet stands firmly on its own two feet. "Mau-Olhado" is an explosive opener with shades of Van der Graaf Generator, subverting time signatures and meters to make way for the vocal sections. "Colosso" brings us jazz-rock, but with vocals, lending it the feel of an auteur band; it is progressive, certainly fusion-oriented, and reminded me of the Argentine group Pez (in their prime). There are layered nuances and shifting moods that subtly overlap within the same track, featuring arrangements that are expertly crafted and perfectly placed. The parade of echoes continues, Gentle Giant makes an appearance, and the quintet shifts from pure jazz to a fierce, aggressive jazz-fusion that catches both the album and the listener off guard, never letting go."Taxidermia" continues the sonic revolution with the Moog front and center, yet the vocal sections are guttural, raw, and fierce, as if a stuffed animal had come to life and started speaking... like a dark sequence from a Lars von Trier film. However, classical piano notes bring light to the darkness, and a guitar with real character tests out a solo before the organ and that otherworldly, sepulchral voice return, creating a striking final contrast. There is a wealth of textures and colors, much like the album cover, which resembles an oil painting just waiting to be touched and felt.The album carries the scent of perfume... yet also the taste of earth, heaven, and hell. "Bode Expiat�rio" blends indigenous Brazilian sounds into that progressive cocktail; there are synthesizers, but also flute and harm�nica, elements of fire and air, alongside the kind of academic exploration associated with Egberto Gismonti.Celeste represents the other side of Brazil, that subtle, often overlooked facet found in the collaborations of Hermeto Pascoal and Edu Lobo or the early work of Sergio Mendes. Papangu surrounds themselves with an array of percussion and a vast arsenal of keyboards to craft a rich, surprisingly varied sound, much like the country's flora and fauna, which inevitably find their way into the compositions. The interplay of percussion continues in "Fechamento de Corpo," accompanied by guitar and flute, yet tradition and homage are disrupted by the intrusion of raw, high-energy rock sections; it is as if wild animals have once again taken control. It is in this stark contrast, which ultimately comes together seamlessly, that the band's spirit and artistic vision truly reside, all while incorporating technology to add textural depth.Calado (de Olho) plays with distortion, genre-blending, high-pitched vocals, and a mix of jazz and psychedelia in a way that reminded me of Gal Costa's early work, truly daring and accomplished, where the only rule was breaking with preconceptions.At times, Iamanakaru hints at certain Zeuhl-like facets, then plays with tradition at the start of "Afirma��o" before brazenly shifting into a markedly atonal progressive rock, almost ritualistic in nature. That is precisely where the magnetism of both the album and the band lies: they do not wait for the listener to come to them; instead, they come to us, right up to the farewell, which features a playful nod and a sort of Bossa Nova, but crafted in a space-age, symphonic style, as it could not have been otherwise.
items._cn_summary: 巴西五人乐队Papangu的专辑《Celestial》以实验精神为骨架，将前卫金属、爵士摇滚与巴西本土音乐语言交织在一起。作品以爆炸性的器乐段落开场，频繁颠覆节拍与拍号结构，Moog合成器与粗粝人声交替形成强烈张力，古典钢琴与暗色调形成对照。专辑融入巴西原住民音乐元素，包括笛子与口琴，配合大量打击乐器与键盘编配，呼应Egberto Gismonti与Hermeto Pascoal的学术探索传统。多首曲目在纯爵士、激烈爵士融合与原始摇滚之间突然切换，野生动物般的不羁能量与精心编排的层次并存，形成独特的艺术张力。整张专辑在元素与情绪之间不断转换，既有天国的轻盈，也有大地的粗粝，展现了乐队跨越传统与现代、本土与前卫的宽广视野。

items.album: “Intimately rustic”: Motvind festival reviewed
items.excerpt: What began as an arts funding protest has grown into a constellation of site-specific performances at this rural Norwegian event, writes Peter Margasak in The Wire 511 Motvind Various venues, Rollag, Norway Thanks to limited resources and modest aims, small summer festivals all across Europe adapt a simple formula: programme a couple of touring acts and round things out with local musicians. items.body: What began as an arts funding protest has grown into a constellation of site-specific performances at this rural Norwegian event, writes Peter Margasak in The Wire 511 Motvind Various venues, Rollag, Norway Thanks to limited resources and modest aims, small summer festivals all across Europe adapt a simple formula: programme a couple of touring acts and round things out with local musicians. But in Norway some of the locals are as compelling and strong as the imported headliners. As terrific as sets by Horse Lords, Bitchin Bajas and Separatist Party may be, the rest of the stylistically broad line-up at Motvind festival never feels secondary. Held in a remote valley a few hours north west of Oslo, the intimately rustic event has morphed from a political protest against the sponsorship of the nearby Kongsberg Jazz Festival by a weapons manufacturer back in 2016 into a celebration of hand-crafted music instilled with a strong improvisational aesthetic, regardless of genre. The organisers don’t need to reach far to find musicians embodying this practice, and most of the performers are part of several overlapping communities. The music unfolds on two nearby stages – a wooden amphitheatre and a tented shelter up the hill – but nothing feels less than intimate. The Sheriffs Of Nothingness – the veteran string duo of violist Ole Henrik Moe and violinist Kari Rønnekleiv – play amid the audience on the amphitheatre stage, where listeners can absorb every microscopic, unamplified sound they produce. The locked in musicians make minimalist sound studies where the grain of every gesture is audible. Many sets are concerned with sound qua sound, whether the austerity of The Sheriffs or the just intonation chamber jazz of Krise, a quartet led by guitarist Kristian Enkerud Lien, where harmonies generated with keyboardist Anna Ueland and trombonist Emil Bø complement soaring, almost epic compositions given a rickety charm by drummer Bjørn André Syverinson. Horse Lords deploy the same tuning during their jacked-up set, and when the group need to adjust tunings they test the patient listeners by extending set pieces – a bracing cascade of feedback and sparkling harmonics from guitarist Owen Gardner, a sculptural carpet of swooping 3D synthesis from bassist Max Eilbacher – into epic textural explorations over Sam Haberman’s jagged beats. The crowd remain with them all the way. Oudist Aly Eissa of The Handover plays a riveting solo set blending self-composed material that embraces Arabic classical tradition with several traditional pieces where he reveals that he can sing just as beautifully as he plucks his instrument. The purity and focus of his performance contrasts with the way the astonishing Pakistani vocalist Muslim Shaggan constantly interrupts the flow of his performance by pedantically explaining every symbol, gesture and shape of what follows. On Sunday afternoon most attendees and performers partake in a soundwalk, traipsing alongside the Numedalslågen river, serenaded by random improvisations along the trail. Crossing over a primitive suspension bridge in groups of five, the audience eventually gather in a nearby park to eat sour porridge and take in a lovely solo performance of traditional Hardanger fiddle music by Johanne Flottorp. Part of a genuinely engaging, hours-long jam session, the finale comes from the Norwegian quartet Lotus with saxophonist Signe Emmeluth, guitarist Karl Bjorå and drummer Olaf Olsen. When their leader and electric bassist Chris Holm becomes unavailable earlier in the day, double bassist Johannes Elnan not only steps into the breach, but his furious playing transforms the band’s highly interactive attack over krautrock grooves into an unstoppable force. This review appears in The Wire 511 along with many other reviews of new and recent records, books, films, festivals and more. To read them all, pick up a copy of the magazine in our online shop. Wire subscribers can also read the issue in our online magazine library.

items._cn_summary: Motvind 音乐节位于挪威奥斯陆西北的偏远山谷，2016年因抗议附近爵士节接受武器制造商赞助而诞生，如今已演变为一场聚焦手工制作与即兴美学的乡村音乐聚会。乐评重点描述了多个演出：小提琴与中提琴二重奏 Sheriffs Of Nothingness 在木质露天剧场中以非扩音方式演奏极简声音研究；Krise 四重奏以纯律室乐爵士呈现从极简到史诗感的作品；Horse Lords 使用相同调律系统进行扩展性声音探索，吉他与贝斯的反馈与合成器纹理被延展为长篇织体实验。埃及裔乌德琴手 Aly Eissa 将阿拉伯古典传统与传统曲目融合为引人入胜的独奏。音乐节强调场地亲密度与社群联系，两座舞台间的转换自然流畅，多元风格共享同一审美底色。

items.body:
“The thing about playing the tuba in an orchestra is that you don’t have to play that much,” admitted composer Matthew Wright, who grew up playing the tuba in orchestras and funk bands, “but it’s the best seat in the house. You hear music back to front. The percussion and the brass are loud, so you hear all their detail, and the strings are this kind of ethereal thing that’s off in the distance.”

For the Kent-based Wright, who also improvises using turntables, samplers, and processers – most impactfully with Trance Map, his partnership with Evan Parker – this early realization nurtured a sensibility leading to the creation of immersive works that mix composition, improvisation, and technology. Cracked Glaze (False Walls) is a case in point, as it utilizes notated material – “dot music” is his good-humored term – improvisation, and Wright’s real-time sampling and processing immediately fed into surround sound, all of which he remixed for the CD.

Wright’s collaborators on Cracked Glaze represent various facets of his work. Ensemble Klang, an ensemble of mostly Dutch new music virtuosi, was an early champion of Wright’s compositions. Spheric Totemic is a Wright-instigated, flexibly configured improvising group with, on this occasion, Mandhira de Saram, Alexander Hawkins, Neil Charles and Stephen Davis. Sofia Jernberg, whose Musho with Hawkins was one of the brighter lights of 2024, is new to Wright’s constellation.

Historically, the conventional wisdom among exponents of freely improvised music is that the larger the group, the more apt the music will be muddied. It is a yardstick that is also prevalent among practitioners of contemporary composition. Individuality – of the improviser, of the composer – is more difficult to assert in or through a crowd. Although there are more than a dozen musicians heard on Cracked Glaze, there is no nebulous sprawl or complexity for complexity’s sake. Abstraction is tethered to figuration, the spine of the piece being a descending line that repeatedly submerges and reemerges, giving the interactions of voices clear relationships.

“In a lot of my written work for ensembles there is a central concern that tends to last a long period of time, an idea that will give the piece structure. I’m really interested in music being a kind of terrain that you can hear through and around, so that when you are listening, you are experiencing a kind of ‘visual’ situation. I guess this goes back to my work with vinyl records, because records make music a physical surface, where you can place the needle anywhere in the terrain of the music.

“In the improvised work, I don’t want to be the guy that says to improvisers, ‘this is how it goes.’ Improvisation, in a free context, is about distributed leadership. It’s about this beautiful situation of people saying, ‘the music could go here’ or ‘I hear the future of this music in what you’re playing,’ and the kind of listening that leads to those sorts of situations.

“Having the opportunity to work with a group that is mainly readers – Ensemble Klang – and a group that is mainly improvisers – Spheric Totemic – and Sofia Jernberg, gave me the opportunity to do something I haven’t done much of in my music, to have a spine that is unfurling but is always there. It doesn’t necessarily always have to be the main focus of the piece, but it will always be there. It will structure time in a certain way; improvisers can do whatever they want to do, and the music will be as much about them as it is the spine. I was really interested in having a sort of ‘object’ in the space of the improvisation. It’s almost like in the visual art world, where you have people moving around in a gallery but there’s a sculpture there. It’s in the room with you.”

Another virtue of Cracked Glaze is that it is the type of work that initially seems to come out of nowhere. It smacks of singularity. However, Wright’s backstory reveals that he did not come out of nowhere, as he has a pedigree linking him to England’s most consequential institutional incubator of experimental music, as well as its most venerable, living exponent of improvised music. Both associations largely account for how Wright’s disparate interests – several of which were common among Gen Xers in their formative years but were delayed in being assimilated into experimental music – were shaped into a mature aesthetic, and yielded in Cracked Glaze an arguably definitive statement.

“My experience, first of all, was writing music and playing in brass bands and funk bands and small improvising groups with friends,” Wright recently explained. “But I also liked writing chamber music for people who would take it away and play it somewhere else. I might not even be there for the performance. This background took me to study at the University of Huddersfield with the Professor who set up the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival, Richard Steinitz. I was very lucky. It was kind of random. He was my composition teacher. So, I was very lucky to have experiences like knocking on the door for a composition lesson and Richard Steinitz saying, ‘Ah, Matt, I can’t possibly teach you right now, but meet Karlheinz,’ and the door opens and there’s this world-famous composer from another generation that I had read about, but never dreamed I would meet.

“Contemporary classical music was a big part of my education, but I DJed as a kid. I was really interested at that point in the ‘80s and ‘90s when software, sampling, and DJ technology, was becoming affordable. It started showing up in people’s homes. Contemporary classical music and DJ culture were colliding in my mind when I was a kid. The only kind of formal education I could get was a classical education, along with some jazz theory, but it was largely based on dot music, written music. Then there was this other (non-written) side, like DJ culture and all of the great heritage of Black music that DJ culture is part of, and that was a kind of informal education I studied for myself.

“When I was a real little kid – like 12 or 13 – I made a lot of bedroom productions with a basic computer and turntable setup, really focused on instrumental hip-hop. I started to scratch around then, just watching how it was done on TV. My main inspirations were DJ Premier of Gangstarr, Terminator X of Public Enemy, and Maseo of De La Soul. When I was around 18 or 19, as a student, I DJed for a few parties, playing mainly funk, hip hop, and drum ‘n' bass. Around the same time – 1996-98 – I was in a few pop/funk bands that needed a DJ, so I did a few things with beat juggling and matching the pitch of the horns with turntable scratches, etc.

“In 1999 I DJed for a social event at the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival and I decided to just play fragments of music that I loved at the time: The Jazz Warriors, Louis Andriessen, Loose Tubes, Squarepusher, Björk. On the basis of that weird mix, I got the call to DJ at Abbey Road for the launch of a music charity, the PRS Foundation, in 2000. That was both a social event and included some (not entirely successful!) experimental scratching. When I moved to Holland to study with composer Louis Andriessen in 2002, I joined a trio with laptop artist Tom Tlalim and saxophonist Keir Neuringer – now of Irreversible Entanglements – and we played a few house parties and small gigs with our own mix of free improv and beat-based electronica. That same year the Huddersfield Festival commissioned ‘Presents from an Edited Then’ which was a 70-minute piece for The Apollo Saxophone Quartet and me DJing, designed for a club venue, again a mix of ‘social’ and ‘experimental’. That’s when I got interested in the worlds of contemporary classical music and DJ culture colliding.”

One of the first projects Wright embarked on was to compose for turntables and to teach classically-trained percussionists how to use them, integrating John Cage’s early work for percussion with the innovations of Christian Marclay and Otomo Yoshihide. “In a piece called Contact Theatre I had literally written out all of the material for notation-reading percussionists”, Wright said of the work. “If you look at a musical stave with the four spaces between the lines, I used those spaces to represent the four spaces on a vinyl record. The space that would be a F in the treble stave, that’s the space on the outer edge of the record, before any musical material appears on the vinyl record. All of the musical material on the record is included in the second space, and then the space at the center of the record was the third space, and then the label itself in the fourth space. You can prepare those spaces, put stickers on them. I would literally write percussion rhythms and they could produce those rhythms by dropping the needle on the record and get a ricochet effect or specify a section of the record I want to be played, say a saxophone solo three minutes into the record. I developed these ‘half-contact’ techniques where the needle sticks like a locked groove, and I taught the basics of hip hop scratching to percussionists, even though the music didn’t sound anything like hip hop.”

Wright then began to assess the proportions of and the relationships between the elements of his aesthetic and how to integrate them in his work. “Cracked Glaze is a collision of all of the above. I have been doing ensemble work and turntable work and installation work, but a lot of my focus is on the work with Evan in mixing and even post-production of the Trance Map material. Post-production is really part of the process, and Evan is very interested in exploring all that. Although Cracked Glaze doesn’t involve Evan, it brings to equal terms all of the sources I work with. There’s some notation written for Ensemble Klang with holes in that notation, space for the improvisation group of Spheric Totemic and Sofia Jernberg. They have start and stop times for the improvising, and they also sometimes have cues for some notation. I’m also mixing them live on stage, taking samples and remixing them and using the turntable as well. Then I take all that material and work on it a little in the studio, not to radically change the piece but to bring out some of the elements that you would hear live but not in a stereo recording. The piece brings together notation, improvisation, and technology, but not as separate forms. They all intersect. That’s where they all join on the map.”

In a roundabout way, the title of the piece speaks to the processes of its creation. It refers to the glazes used in high-fire ceramics that are formulated to crack on temperature; even though they are applied in an even manner, the cracking results in a surface that can be likened to a mosaic assembled with random tiles, with dark, hair-thin spaces between them. Though the results are subject to a unique firing, the experienced artist knows how to promote cracking that is pleasing and avoid cracking that ruins the piece.

“It may be interesting to talk about how jazz standards have worked in the past,” Wright responded to the idea of controlled cracking, and chuckling at the notion that he controlled the gas valve. “An excellent standard is one that can be played in its entirety and feel integrated and beautiful, but it is also a catalyst. It offers itself up to be cracked, to be turned into something new. In some ways, the use of notation to suggest a response is fascinating to me. On a technical level, there are definitely moments where I say to the improvisers, ‘at a certain point you will hear a line and at that point, that pitch, that’s your moment; if you’re improvising, the natural ebb and flow of the group will go to you’. But I don’t say ‘you should crack it’ to them; I say ‘it’s yours’.

“And there’s a third element there, the equivalent of the heat – the processing and the spatialization. I’m taking the feed of everybody, the notated music and the improvised music is coming to my setup, and I’m able to remix it and sample it. I’m an agent in the cracking, too. Whether it is notated or not is not the point, because it’s all going through the same system and being splintered into surround sound. That’s the third element, the sound design is a catalytic element.”

Wright pointed to a poster in his studio of a still influential Japanese textile exhibition he attended in his early 20s. “What I loved about that,” he said, “was that the dynamic shapes of these textiles are very rigid, spatially, but the textiles themselves have all sorts of holes in them. They are almost like fishing nets. I tried to create something similar by creating a structure that’s flexible but has holes in it. If we play this piece again, the melody line and the structure is going to be exactly the same every time and the improvising and the specialization will be different every time. That’s a long-winded way of saying I tried not to over notate.”

Wright acknowledged that post-production, particularly when the work was created in a surround sound environment and is remixed for stereo, creates a distinct experience of the work, and perhaps represents a new iteration of the pursuit of perfection in the studio, exemplified by Glenn Gould. “My pieces are concepts that have a sort of quantum existence,” Wright maintained. “What I mean is that if we are going to present the piece live, then there are circumstances that will be dynamic for the audience in the live space that may not be so dynamic when hearing it at home. In the live space, I’m dealing with surround sound. There are a whole lot of options to try to present that sort of experience in the stereo format. When it comes to making a CD or something online that people will listen to, I consider the domestic setting. I also consider that many people listen to music on the go, with headphones or their phone. You may be walking down the Avenue of the Americas and everything around you is changing, but there’s one consistent thread in the music.

“You have to consider the multiple ways that people listen now. I do hope that people will sit at home to listen to it. In that situation, it’s much closer to reading a book because it’s a solitary experience. You’re sitting with it for 40 or 50 minutes. Wearing headphones creates an interior experience. I really treasure those kinds of listeners and it’s a real privilege when someone spends that time with something that I’ve made with my musical friends.

“In the history of improvised music there have been many vehement statements about the relationship between free improvised music and recording. I totally get that, but I suppose that the question we now have to consider is what happens when you improvise with a recording. We don’t want the karaoke thing! How does the recording come back into the improvised music experience in as fluid a way you would have with another musician with an instrument? An instrument is obviously a technology of its own and the recording is the result of the technology. We need to make sure the technology is as flexible as any other instrument. The other thing I’m really fascinated by in the history of free creative music is the evolution of incorporating electronics. It’s really interesting for me when an electro-acoustic improvised situation might suggest that the music is not happening in the present tense, but in the past or the future.

“The thing I’m really interested in is those previously separated camps of notation, improvisation, and technology becoming one and the same, where there is an equaling out of the three. You’re not relying on one form of expression. And this seems to be causing a real revitalization of the scene, where people are mastering their separate disciplines and are also negotiating with each other. I think there’s more opportunity for creative music because of the dialogue between notation, improvisation, and technology. Looking for the connections between them is the main creative impetus. It’s not paper; it’s not technology; it’s not adherence to one way of making music. It’s about thinking about the connections between the people you’re working with. Saying ‘all of the above’ may be too easy an answer, but it does ascribe equal value to notation, improvisation and technology. These are all zones on the map and they all overlap each other, so the paths between those zones are what I’m interested in.”

***

Wright’s projects frequently overlap, the post production of one coinciding with the development of another. With summer approaching, Wright was mixing a duo session with Pat Thomas that has the flavor of This is Trickster; a Spheric Totemic album, and a Trance Map + recording on which Parker and him are joined by harpist Milana Zaric and Richard Barrett.

The presence of Barrett is particularly intriguing, as he pioneered improvised electronic music beginning in the 1990s – largely through FURT, his partnership with Paul Obermayer – laying groundwork for Wright and others. Additionally, Barrett’s compositions are renowned for testing – and often surpassing – the presumed physical limits of instrumentalists.

Barrett and Wright are part of a trajectory of composers foregrounding technology in their work. An earlier dot on the line, one that is essential but not obvious, is Conlon Nancarrow. The expatriate composer is the inspiration for Wright’s next major work, “Passing Nancarrow.” Wright’s latest project with the Belgian ensemble BL!NDMAN (the exclamation point is intentional) also has Hawkins in a key role. The piece debuts next year, marking 30 years since Nancarrow died.

“The idea of the piece is based around Nancarrow being obsessed with Art Tatum’s playing,” Wright explained. “He sampled Tatum in the form of piano rolls, using technology from a hundred years ago. What we will do is, while Alex improvises in real time, his notes are captured and this will trigger all sorts of reactions from the group. In a way, we turn Alex’s music into a piano roll.”

Wright was partly inspired by the writer and documentary film director Helen Borton’s comment that jazz and blues collide like a “hurricane” in Nancarrow’s music. Replace “hurricane” with “Nancarrow” and you get the gist of Wright’s conceptualization for the recording he is currently mixing – “four hurricanes of all kinds of crazy sounds.” Wright also considered the music of Squarepusher, Aphex Twin, and other exponents of electronic dance music, that influenced him when Nancarrow died in 1997, leading him to include “strange, intelligent dance music in the piece.”

However, the nexus of Nancarrow, Barrett, and Wright, is the consideration of the limits of music humans can create in real time, and how to get to the edge of those limits, if not extend them.

“Nancarrow reached for impossible, post-human music. But in my current work, I don’t have an artistic interest in post-human AI. I’ve heard a lot of AI-generated music and read a lot of AI research, and the thing I’m already bored by is that AI can do almost anything. Like a musician that can play everything and just won’t stop playing to give space for others, AI doing anything and everything is boring to me when you don’t hear inspired choices and you don’t hear the human labor or the human need for considered space in the music. But, I’m open minded. I just haven’t heard anything that inspires me yet. Back to the human level, in Alex’s piano playing, there is that reaching beyond what is supposedly humanly possible, to reach a new vista for what is possible.

“You can say that, for his times, Nancarrow was making a post-human kind of music, but we should remember that he sat there, punching holes. So, I don’t hear a sort of pre-AI in his music, a piano that can do anything, but the blood and the hours of Nancarrow sitting maybe six months to create an explosive two minutes. I want to know how humans feel when they hear music and when they make music. If that is aided by technology, the idea is that the technology helps musical thinking like an instrument helps musical thinking. My interest in technology is the same as Alex’s interest in the piano, there’s a tradition of human tool use there that in a sense heightens the human listening experience if done successfully.

“Another thing I like about Nancarrow was that he was true to his beliefs, which is why he left the US for Mexico City, which resulted in him working in relative isolation. He just got on with it. A few people had experimented with the player piano before, but he made it his own. I appreciate that you can hear the edges in music and you’re OK with not being able to know everything beyond that edge. I guess the difference between the scene we have now and Nancarrow’s situation is that we can go to the edge together in a collaborative spirit.”

items._cn_summary: 作曲家Matthew Wright的专辑《Cracked Glaze》将记谱作曲、自由即兴与实时电子采样处理融为一体，所有素材经环绕声录制后由他重新混缩为CD版本。Wright早年作为乐团大号手积累了独特的听觉视角，后转向唱机、采样器与处理器，尤其在与Evan Parker合作的Trance Map项目中展现出对声音物质性的敏感。专辑邀集十余位音乐人参与，包括荷兰新音乐团体Ensemble Klang、灵活配置的即兴乐团Spheric Totemic，以及与Alexander Hawkins有过出色合作的Sofia Jernberg。面对如此庞大的编制，Wright以一条反复沉浮的下行旋律线作为结构脊柱，使抽象与具象相互牵引，避免了大型自由即兴常见的混沌松散。他将即兴视为分布式领导——不预设方向，而是让参与者从彼此的演奏中听见音乐的未来走向，并将记谱比作唱片凹槽中的地形，暗示音乐是一种可以被穿越和环绕的可视空间。
