items.body: It took no less than nine years for the new opus from Swiss band Sleepwalk to arrive. Founder Bruno Rush, assisted by Andreas Lehmann, has prepared 15 new tracks for “Dystopia”. An additional disc featuring no fewer than 17 is also available. To say the wait was long is an understatement, but it was certainly worth it. The result, “Dystopia”, is truly impressive. Sleepwalk’s compositions straddle the line between EBM and Dark-Electro. The songwriting is highly sophisticated, backed by an impressive sonic arsenal. The atmosphere is dark and the rhythms are danceable, while the tracks manage to be complex yet accessible. On the standout tracks—and there are quite a few—you can hear influences from the early Canadian EBM school; I am thinking specifically of the genius of Skinny Puppy. The opening tracks, in particular, absolutely blew me away and, in my opinion, rank among the best material Sleepwalk has ever produced. Given that the band has been active since 1992 and has a substantial back catalogue, the long wait has truly paid off. Sleepwalk hasn’t reinvented itself; rather, they seem to have taken a step back to reflect on their future direction. Lehmann’s haunting vocals fit the album’s atmosphere and genre perfectly. Towards the end, a few more magnificent tracks emerge, evoking the sound of Front Line Assembly. And then, of course, there’s the bonus disc, featuring 14 bands, each contributing a cover of a Sleepwalk song, plus three remixes by three different bands. It’s quite unusual to see so many bands featured with covers rather than remixes, and the least I can say is that it’s a very original idea—and it works. There’s also a fine lineup of artists assembled here, including labelmates such as Pyroline, Trilogy, T.A.N.K., Serpents, and Synaptic Defect, as well as EBM scene veterans such as Plastic Noise Experience, Brain Leisure, Individual Totem, R010R, Pantser Fabriek, To Avoid, and others. I have to say, there are some brilliant songs to be heard. Plastic Noise Experience does a fantastic job on “Afterlife,” and I should also mention Individual Totem, Synaptic Defect, and Nine Seconds. “Dystopia” is an album with a strong nostalgic streak, yet one that has been successfully translated into a powerful, contemporary sound: tormented EBM featuring some highly danceable tracks. Sleepwalk is back, and the world is going to know it. Side-Line announced the release in April 2026 in Sleepwalk return with ‘Dystopia’ 2CD on Electro Aggression Records, which listed the 2CD and digital editions and the full remix roster of the bonus disc “Interpretations”. (Rating:8½). Listen to “Devil In Disguise”: Devil in Disguise by Sleepwalk About Sleepwalk Sleepwalk are a dark electro and EBM act from Bern, Switzerland. The project was founded in 1992 by Oliver Spring and Bruno Ruch, Andreas Lehmann, and Charly of tEaR!doWn. The group started releasing material in the early 1990s, including “Immortal Disease” from 1994, the first album “Door To Insomnia…” in 1995 on Khazad-Dûm, “Black Diagnose” in 1999, “Torture Chamber” in 2002, “Retrospect 94-96 (The Early Years)” in 2003, and “Rapid Eye Movement” on Scanner in March 2004. By the mid-2000s the lineup had shifted. Oliver Spring left the band in 2005. The band later released the EP “Revenge Of The Lost” in 2011 and the concept album “Nibiru” in 2012, both on Scanner. Sleepwalk joined Electro Aggression Records to release “Tempus Vincit Omnia” on January 3, 2018. The band said they wanted to move back toward more classic dark electro with EBM influence after “Nibiru”. The Bandcamp-only digital set “Remakes”, issued on April 11, 2026, revisited older Sleepwalk tracks ahead of “Dystopia”, the 2CD set reviewed here.
items._cn_summary: 瑞士乐队Sleepwalk沉寂九年后推出的双碟专辑《Dystopia》，由创始人Bruno Ruch与Andreas Lehmann合作完成，收录15首新作加一张17轨翻唱附碟。乐评指出作品游走于EBM与暗电子之间，编曲成熟、节奏强劲且适合舞池，既复杂又不失可听性。开篇几首被认为是乐队迄今最佳制作，受早期加拿大EBM（尤其是Skinny Puppy）影响明显，尾段则让人联想到Front Line Assembly的声响质感。附碟《Interpretations》汇集十四个乐队翻唱及三首混音，阵容覆盖Plastic Noise Experience、Synaptic Defect等圈内老将，以翻唱而非混音为主的形式被评价为颇具原创性。整体而言，专辑在怀旧与当代之间找到了平衡，将阴暗氛围与可跳舞的律动统一在统一的制作框架中。

items.body: After the brutal heatwaves of August, the chilly depths of winter feel like a distant threat. But signs of the creeping cold are slowly emerging; cooling nights, the return of pumpkin spice, a dwindling tomato season. For those ready for the crisp return of colder weather, there’s Convulsif’s latest album, which is slowly unfolding like the change of seasons. Today, a new glimpse is unveiled. Fittingly, “A Torch Then Blaze” is something of a transitional track on Anatomy of Rage. A quick, bass-heavy interlude that emerges with sinister intent and lurching grooves spliced with grinding noise that connects the blistering first chapter with the funeral pyres of the middle tracks.While short, “A Torch Then Blaze” illustrates the fascinating juxtapositions created by Convulsif: maximalist experiments constrained within minimalist production, chaotic noise rock sharpened to a razor’s edge. Rather than embrace the massive production often found in experimental rock, Convulsif keeps their sound centered and brutally direct. Structure loses all meaning - songs range from 76 seconds to nearly 20 minutes - allowing tightly coiled grooves and jagged, jazzy rhythms to take control. The clarity creates a menacing beast of noise and abrasion, one that’s encapsulated by the brief warning siren of “A Torch Then Blaze” as it groans and explodes into noisy flames. Anatomy of Rage will be released on October 1, 2026. Pre-order on Bandcamp and follow the band via their website.

items._cn_summary: 这篇文章是对乐队 Convulsif 新专辑《Anatomy of Rage》中单曲《A Torch Then Blaze》的试听首播介绍。文章以季节更替为隐喻引入音乐氛围，将其描述为短小精悍的过渡曲目，以低沉贝斯和研磨式噪音为核心，在张狂失序与极简结构之间取得平衡。乐评指出乐队刻意避开大型制作呈现，而采用中心化的、直接的声音呈现方式，强调音轨长度从76秒到近20分钟不等，结构本身被打破，由紧密缠绕的律动与棱角分明的爵士化节奏驱动。从风格描述来看，作品融合了噪音、暗黑氛围与实验摇滚元素，在极简框架内展现密集的声响层次，与暗潮及实验音乐口味有较高契合度。文章末尾提及发行日期与Bandcamp预购链接，属于试听首播性质的推介内容。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The trio dynamic is further developed in this new foray into the ambiguous territory between rock, electronica, and the smooth yet steady interplay of synthesizers, guitar, and bass.This is how "Before Dawn" unfolds; as "Reach For Tomorrow" begins, a touch of improvisation, at once symphonic and psychedelic, weaves through the programmed tracks (which simultaneously mimic a choir). It would not be a stretch to detect echoes of both the classic style of Klaus Schulze like the modern style of Annie Clark from the band St. Vincent."Clouds" seems to feature a Mellotron, yet when the vibraphone and glockenspiel chime alongside the unhurried guitar notes, they evoke the quiet interludes found between Robert Fripp's dark, aggressive solos of the past, as if King Crimson had been stripped of its outer shell to reveal a vulnerable core usually kept protected. Above all, the approach taken in "The Only Way To Find You" is consistently tranquil and reflective, though perhaps not deeply profound, seemingly waiting to be imbued with whatever the listener brings to it. Like the rest of the album, "How Long Have You Remembered" reflects the marshmallow hues of the cover art, creating a somewhat surreal atmosphere; at times, James's style suggests a blend of the playful Talking Heads and the contrapuntal guitar work of R.E.M., while "Olen Yksin" features guest vocalist Laura Naukkarinen, whose ethereal presence underscores the postmodern aura of both the album and the trio.There is also a touch of Air, the French duo that successfully married electronica with 70s symphonic sounds. "Turn Turn, Round Here" returns with a hint of distortion to reassert the indie character of their sound; drifting amidst various textures, the track finds its natural rhythm, almost like a metronome, while the drums quicken and a Moog-like sound zigzags through the remainder of the song, heightening the dreamlike atmosphere.You can hear echoes of Kraftwerk, amidst the Rhodes piano and drums, with notes reminiscent of early computer sounds slipping through the interstices of a slowly built wall of sound, as subtle as the passage of time itself. That same sense of time accelerates electronically on "Don't Be Shy," where, much like Brian Eno, they manage to blend electronics with a rock sensibility, creating a piece that feels warm and emotive at times, even within a minimalist setting.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑在摇滚、电子与合成器之间构建了一片模糊地带。三件乐器与编程音色交织出层叠的织体，键盘音色模拟合唱效果，史密斯式的合成器与吉他对位呼应，营造出安静而内省的整体氛围。梅洛特朗与颤音琴的点缀增添了梦幻质感，而末段则引入失真与模块化合成器的声音，使专辑在迷幻与极简之间来回摆动。歌词方面引用芬兰语歌词，由客座女声演唱，强化了后现代气质。整体而言，制作精细，情绪偏冥想式，但缺乏更深层的颠覆性。

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 984Porcupine Tree is an English progressive rock band that was formed in 1987 in Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire. The fourth studio album of Porcupine Tree "Signify" that was released in 1996 is their first album with a fixed line up. Steven Wilson previously used various musicians to shape his compositions. "Signify" shows a clear transition phase from the band with the long instrumental tracks and lots of musical experiments to the more song orientated band. "Signify" presents a more mature approach than on "The Sky Moves Sideways", which doesn't mean better, having a stronger mix of styles. This is a relaxed work, generally slow and that doesn't have many hooks for the listener to grab on to. Its psychedelic sound is more ambient than ever, but I think isn't as deep as the wonderful "The Sky Moves Sideways".The line up on "Signify" is Steven Wilson (vocals, electric and acoustic guitars, samplers, tapes, organ, Mellotron, piano, drum programming, chimes and musical box), Richard Barbieri (piano, Hammond organ, tapes, sequencers and synthesizers Prophet-V and Roland System 700), Colin Edwin (bass and double bass guitars) and Chris Maitland (vocals, drums, cymbals, percussion, drum loops and keyboards. The work had the participation of Terumi (vocals) too.The original version of "Signify" has twelve tracks. "Signify" begins with "Bornlivedie" in which a narrator invites us to make ourselves comfortable to enjoy a soundscape that culminates with a female voice saying "Signify". "Signify" is the title track, where we actually can say that the album begins. It's an incredible paranoia inducing track, a hard riff, a pure electronic wonder and where a simple distorted solo from Wilson gives the atmosphere and rhythm. "The Sleep Of No Dreaming", as most of the songs of the album, has a very dark and brooding feel with lyrics chilling and sharp. It's a contrasting composition with the previous instrumental with quiet chords on the keyboards that set the dreamy mood for the track. "Pagan" is a quick transitory piece. It's a soundscape, an atmospheric piece, a guiding element between one theme and another. "Waiting Phase One" and "Waiting Phase Two" take up just over ten minutes. The first part starts with some acoustic chords and a few beats on the bass drum creating a peaceful moment, a kind of different peace. The second part is tribally enchanting due to the variety of sounds that emerge from it with a brief phrase on the piano and the tuneful touch on the guitar. The percussion and drums stand out within this psychedelic trance. "Sever" is where the harder progressive rock meets the electronic music. Maitland and Edwin are simply spectacular. It has a great chorus, with distorted voices crying out in despair, which makes this song another highlight on the album. "Idiot Prayer" has a pure electronic ambient. The band again approaches a different style and shows how eclectic they can be. Over a danceable rhythm, the guitar and keyboards move gracefully equally supported by an attractive percussion. "Every Home Is Wired" is a song that sounds more like a "Stupid Dream" or a "Lightbulb Sun" track. Here we have guitar and dreamlike keyboards under some echoing voices. Again the band is showing that this album can have it all. "Intermediate Jesus" is one of the biggest tracks on the album. It sounds like a kind of a jam that was included in the final material. This is an interesting instrumental, mostly improvisation, the only collective composition on the album. "Light Mass Prayers" is another ambient piece, but much longer than "Pagan". It has an atmospheric beginning, an ambient sound mainly through the keyboards. It's an exploration and experimentation by Wilson. "Dark Matter" is the lengthiest track on the album. It has some of the most brutal lyrics on the album, takes us out with an epic solo and some recollection and deep thought. This beautiful song, so dreamy and so awakening closes the album in a great way.The expanded remastered edition of "Signify" has 2 CD's. It comes with a bonus disc. The supplemental CD consists of demos recorded by the band between 1995-1996. This limited edition contains some extremely well developed, but still rough-on-the-edges demos and outtakes of "Signify". If you have any doubt about the quality of those tracks, rest assured. You don't get filler material here, but a fine complete album, which can hold a candle to the original release.Conclusion: Porcupine Tree occupies a very special place in the field of modern progressive rock and "Signify" is a great example of that. In reality, what we have here is a great addition to any progressive music collection. Basically all facets of the band on only one album are performed in high performance and with rich musicality. Overall, I loved the album and it's a great transition from their psychedelic space rock era, to a more modern progressive rock style which they later perfected. As I said before, "Signify" is the first Porcupine Tree's album where they sound like a band and not a Wilson's "vanity" project. It's a work where they forge their own unique sound and the foundation of their future albums "Stupid Dream" and "In Absentia". Nevertheless, regardless of it not being the best Porcupine Tree's album, this is a highly recommended work. Both challenging and accessible, this album surely has won over some new fans.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: And I see your sadness Is it just like mine? We spend much of life rehearsing permanence. Calendars extend months ahead, plans multiply, and ordinary chores encourage the soothing fiction that tomorrow is already ours. Mortality remains manageable as long as it stays abstract, assigned to strangers or some distant version of ourselves. Grief breaks that arrangement. One absence can make every future date feel provisional, exposing distraction as one of the mind’s most useful shelters. “As We Dance With Tears in The Rain” — Death Drifts Under the Skin in Traitrs Video for “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong” That shelter is nearly universal. Work, desire, entertainment, ambition, and the small obligations of the day let us function while the knowledge of an ending waits at the edge of thought. When that knowledge presses forward, it carries a second fear with it: the possibility of losing every person, object, memory, and role through which we understand ourselves. Continuing to move after facing that fact can become its own form of courage. Toronto coldwave act TRAITRS confronts that contradiction in the new video for “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong,” released last November and later included on the band’s album POSSESSOR; the song begins with private anguish before reaching toward the possibility that another person’s grief may resemble our own. “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong is challenging The Psychology of Ignoring Death.” The recording begins beneath low, echoing synths, its measured dirge already gathering force. A disciplined drumbeat dances in the face of death, pulling the song forward as the guitars climb through serrated sweeps, widening melodies, and mounting sheets of effects. Shawn Tucker’s voice carries the cracked theatricality associated with Robert Smith and Brett Anderson while retaining its own bruised register, rising from a controlled ache toward the sound of a heart crying out against erasure. Each confession lands like a brick dropped onto a bare floor. The verses catalogue bodily harm through blunt images of starvation, wires, poison, and a fatal fall; the chorus turns outward, searching another person’s face for the same sorrow. There is a curious reversal within the arrangement: as the dirge-like synths grow heavier, the song seems to quicken, converting dread into momentum. Midway through, an organ-like phrase drives the track into a broader ascent before cascading vocals and guitars accumulate into a dense wall of sound, carrying the music to its greatest height precisely where the subject closes in on extinction. When the single first appeared, Tucker described the shared recognition at its center: “I felt that song connected me to everything and everyone, it is the one thing we all share and have in common,” Tucker said. “It is also a wake up call to live the life you want to live. We only have one chance at this so go dance in the rain.” Directed by Tucker and filmed in severe black and white, the video places Emmanuelle Vaughan inside a space without visible walls, floor, or horizon. She first appears at a distance beneath a narrow overhead light, nearly motionless, before the camera moves close to her collarbone, spine, hands, and face. An oil-dark coating begins to spread across her fingers, arms, back, and throat as her gestures become more expansive. Between these passages, Tucker performs at the microphone and guitar through smoke, coarse grain, and bands of video interference. Vaughan keeps dancing while her body is gradually claimed by the surrounding black, until the final movements yield to an empty frame. Tucker explains: “I find myself personally active in ignoring mortality. It’s inescapable and we use distraction as defence against it. We all crave purpose and everyday distractions. This is a psychological defense mechanism keeping our deepest fears at bay. Our fight for survival. Death has a way of playing with us, bringing up this deep sense of isolation and failure that we are all constantly running away from. Most people find the concept of being completely alone terrifying and painful. It’s stealing our tomorrows, it steals away everything. This album is incredibly personal for me because I’m still trying to make sense of a major loss in my own life. When I directed this, the goal was to visualize death as this unstoppable force—almost like a terminal illness creeping through the body. It doesn’t care who you are; it just destroys. But I didn’t want the video to just be bleak. It’s about our internal fight. I had wrapped the ‘Burn In Heaven’ video up a few months prior and was thinking about casting for I Was Ill and wanted to work with Emma again on this project as the lead and push her in a completely different approach. I also knew Emma knows exactly what I was looking for, and expected of her. In the video, she is aware death has come, but she still chooses to dance, finding this beautiful defiance right up until the black void completely takes over. It was all shot in one day on location in a small studio warehouse in Hamilton, Ontario, that took 7 hours.” The visual idea draws from Jonathan Glazer’s Under the Skin, particularly its limitless black chamber, where space loses every familiar coordinate and solitude becomes physical. Here, the setting turns mortality into an encroaching presence that can be seen on the body. Vaughan understands what has entered the room, yet her dance continues for as long as movement remains possible. “The void represented Ultimate Isolation perfectly and supports my visual theme of total isolation. There are no walls, no horizons, and no exit. The victims are entirely alone with their desires right before they are destroyed.” Tucker reduces the premise to one plain sentence: “None of us are getting out of here alive.” Within the song and video, that certainty becomes a reason to recognize another person’s sadness, inhabit the present, and dance while the body still answers. Watch the video for “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong” below: Formed in Toronto in 2015, TRAITRS began as a recording project before sessions with producer Josh Korody led to the 2016 debut Rites and Ritual. Butcher’s Coin followed in 2018, expanding the band’s audience across North America and Europe, while 2021’s Horses in the Abattoir brought another set of propulsive rhythms, angular guitars, and horror-informed electronics. Years of touring have carried TRAITRS through more than a dozen countries, including appearances at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Castle Party, and Canadian Music Week, as well as shows with VNV Nation, Lebanon Hanover, She Past Away, Twin Tribes, and Ultra Sunn. POSSESSOR, released March 13, 2026, brings the band’s preoccupation with grief, alienation, and mortality into its most personal form to date. Recorded at Toronto’s Wychwood Studios with Josh Korody and mastered by Matt Colton, the album is available to stream here and order through Bandcamp here. items._cn_summary: 多伦多冷潮乐队TRAITRS在单曲《I Was Ill, You Were Wrong》中探讨死亡意识与人类联结的主题。作品以低沉的回响合成器开场，节制的鼓点在死亡面前起舞，吉他在锯齿状扫弦与层叠音效中攀升。主唱Shawn Tucker的声线带有Robert Smith与Brett Anderson式的破碎戏剧性，在受控的痛苦与抗消失的呐喊之间游走。歌词以饥饿、电线、毒药、致命坠落等直白意象罗列身体伤害，副歌则转向外部，在另一张脸上搜寻相似的哀伤。编曲呈现有趣的倒置：葬礼般的合成器越沉重，音乐越加速，将恐惧转化为动力。中段管风琴般的乐句将歌曲推向更宽阔的攀升，级联的人声与吉他汇聚成密集的音墙，在主题逼近消亡之处抵达最高点。视频由Tucker执导，黑白影像强化了死亡与生存矛盾的核心命题，与用户偏好的暗潮类型高度契合。

items.body: German electronic composer Michael Brückner released “The Egg in the Cosmic Crack” through the Argentine label Cyclical Dreams on 28 August 2026. The album runs six tracks and 77 minutes of Berlin School sequencing and ambient, and is out on digital platforms, as a download and on CD. Two of those tracks are almost twenty years old. The opener “The Egg of Ecquirlo” began as a giveaway Brückner made in 2007 for members of a Last.fm group he had founded, a track he kept meaning to place on a proper album. “Cracked Egg Mystification” came out of the same set of preoccupations and went to the Cerebral Audio compilation “The Rift: Volume 1” in 2016. Both were remixed, partly rearranged, remastered and given new detail for this release. From unused material left over from the 2007 sessions, plus fresh parts, Brückner assembled “The Egg of Ecquirlo – Part 2”, then recorded further pieces to complete the record. The thread running through all of it is a book. Brückner started making music at 21, prompted by meditative yoga practice, and through those studies read Joseph Chilton Pearce’s “The Crack in the Cosmic Egg”. Cyclical Dreams describes the result as “music based on the idea of the egg as a universal symbol”, and the album notes report that those early influences still inform Brückner’s music decades on. There is wordplay underneath the concept. The word “eye” appears in two of the titles, “Joseph’s Eye” and “The Eye of Cyclops”, and sounds like the German “Ei”, meaning egg. Brückner built the album on a wide spread of hardware and software instruments: the Waldorf Blofeld, Behringer DeepMind 6 and Model D, Moog Labyrinth, Korg Z1, NI Absynth, Cherry Audio Rhodes Chroma, GX-80 and Elka-X, u-he Hive 2 and the Moog Theremini. Cyclical Dreams handled the artwork, with photography by Amp Puttipong. The Egg in the Cosmic Crack by Michael Brückner Michael Brückner’s six tracks and where to hear them “The Egg of Ecquirlo – Part 1” (22:23) “Coda (A Pure Oval Shape)” (4:54) “Joseph’s Eye” (13:28) “Cracked Egg Mystification (Revisited)” (13:52) “The Egg of Ecquirlo – Part 2” (10:08) “The Eye of Cyclops” (12:49) The album is on Bandcamp and across digital platforms, with a download edition through Payhip and a CD pressed on demand through the label’s Kunaki storefront. Cyclical Dreams has also put the full album on YouTube. About Michael Brückner Michael Brückner was born in Heidelberg in 1969 and settled near Mainz, where he works as a graphic designer. He began composing and recording electronic music in 1992 without formal training, after the experience of mantra chanting in a yoga group, and started circulating his work through online networks from 2006. His output has run to well over a hundred albums, most of them downloads and CDrs, and he has performed live at smaller festivals and solo since 2012. His music sits mainly in ambient and Berlin School, with long sequenced passages and drifting synth layers. He records with several groups alongside his solo work, including P’Faun, Bridge To Imla and La Mansarde Hérmetique, and has collaborated with Mathias Grassow, Volker Lankow and Mathias Brüssel among others. Brückner has released steadily through Cyclical Dreams, the Buenos Aires label whose catalogue covers Berlin School, ambient, soundscape, space music and drone. His albums for it include “Footprints”, “Recycled Life”, “Twenty-Five Light Years”, “The Morphic Cycle”, “The Seven Planes of Dreams” in 2024 and “A Sequence of Colours” in December 2025. Side-Line has followed the label’s recent output, including D*Time’s “Nightwoven” and Christian Wittman‘s “Andromeda”. “The Egg in the Cosmic Crack” reaches further back than any of them, finishing a piece of music Brückner has carried since 2007.

items.body: Boy Harsher released a lyric video for “Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call)” on 26 August 2026, the third advance single from “Get Mean”, out 18 September 2026 on Atlantic Records. The Northampton duo of Jae Matthews and Augustus Muller follow “Jeans” and “Hard Beat” with a track built around a repeated “I’m OK” and the line “Do you even know my name?”. Los Angeles video artist Sean McGuirk assembled the clip on vintage video gear, styling it as an analog karaoke screen: a CRT television, cold blue background, thick yellow capitals and visible scan lines, with cards reading “IN THE STYLE OF” and “INSTRUMENTAL BREAK”. Jesse Korman shot the footage at PropHaus Brooklyn. What Boy Harsher put on ‘Get Mean’ The album runs twelve tracks: “Ronny”, “Jeans”, “Break Me”, “Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call)”, “Faulty”, “Coming Home”, “Hard Beat”, “Ice Pick (Walk Away)”, “Ivy’s Spiral”, “Pray 4 Me”, “Falling” and “Bleed”. Matthews and Muller recorded it across eight locations in the United States, Mexico and Italy, after Matthews wrote much of the material travelling through West Texas, the Pacific Northwest and South Florida. The pair ended their romantic relationship in early 2024 and the writing period also took in family loss. Matthews has kept her description of the record short. She calls it “what I had to give during the most extreme period of my life.” The sound picks up detuned pads, abrasive synth leads, pedal-steel bends, new wave guitar and unprocessed phone recordings. It is the duo’s first album since the 2022 short film and soundtrack “The Runner”. Atlantic issues “Get Mean” on 140g black vinyl with a 12 x 24 inch poster, on an indie-exclusive blue marble pressing, on a Record Store Day blue variant and on CD. Pre-orders run through Bandcamp via Nude Club Records, the duo’s own imprint, and through record shops. Side-Line covered the signing and the album announcement in Boy Harsher signs to Atlantic Records, announces ‘Get Mean’. The Heartbreak Tour reaches North America from 25 September and Europe and the UK from 14 November, closing in Antwerp on 4 December. Dates in Denver, Paris, Glasgow and Bristol have now sold out, joining the Chicago, Portland, Seattle, Vancouver and Los Angeles shows already gone. The full itinerary is listed in Boy Harsher announce ‘The Heartbreak Tour’ North American dates for 2026. Matthews and Muller have also directed and scored a feature-length horror thriller, “The Lonely Woman”, with a cast including Chloë Sevigny, FKA twigs, Sturgill Simpson, Will Oldham and Jake Weary. About Boy Harsher Jae Matthews and Augustus Muller met at film school in Savannah, Georgia, and began working together in 2013 as Teen Dreamz, with Matthews performing spoken word over Muller’s backing. They took the name Boy Harsher in January 2014 and issued the home-recorded “Lesser Man” EP as a cassette. DKA Records released their first album, “Yr Body Is Nothing”, in 2016, followed by the “Country Girl” EP in 2017 and singles including “Motion”, “Run” and “Face the Fire”. The pair founded their own label, Nude Club, in 2018 and reissued the back catalogue through it. “Pain II” arrived that year with a remix by The Soft Moon. The album “Careful” followed in 2019, with “Country Girl Uncut” and a remix set the same year. Side-Line rated “Careful” 8½ on release. The duo relocated to Northampton, Massachusetts. In January 2022 they released “The Runner”, a short film starring Kristina Esfandiari that streamed on Shudder, together with its soundtrack and the “Burn It Down” EP. Festival appearances between 2022 and 2024 included Primavera Sound, Roadburn, Cruel World and Coachella, and in November 2024 they featured on the Pet Shop Boys double A-side “New London Boy / All The Young Dudes”. Muller also runs Safe Mind with Cooper B. Handy, whose album “Cutting the Stone” appeared on 25 July 2025. Boy Harsher signed to Atlantic Records in July 2026. “Get Mean” is their first album for the label and their first full-length in four years.

items.body: Reinhard Hüber brought T.A.N.K. to life in 2001 as a solo project, later joined by additional members for live performances. After more than 20 years, this is only the third album from the German EBM project. Several years have elapsed between releases, making each album feel somewhat like a new beginning, although I don’t think the EBM audience ever truly forgot T.A.N.K. “Broken Mirror” is the first album in nine years and also the project’s first release on Electro Aggression Records. It features 13 tracks plus five remixes and even a cover version. T.A.N.K. stands for vintage EBM—tracks that drive straight ahead. Typical heavy EBM basslines are paired with dark string arrangements, all set to a danceable rhythm. Here and there, a brief respite appears in the form of a slower tempo, where the EBM takes on a more atmospheric quality. Perhaps slightly atypical is Hüber’s harder, deep, distorted vocal style. While this is more common in Dark Electro productions, it works perfectly here. Among the tracks, I have a particular soft spot for “Zombie March” and its hilarious lyrics. After all, EBM rarely features profound lyrics—and that’s not something I personally expect from the genre anyway! Remixes were provided by Pyrroline, Sleepwalk, Serpents, Synaptic Defect, and Trilogy. The intelligent remix by Pyrroline, in particular, is an absolute treat for the ears. Finally, we get a somewhat surprising cover of R010R’s “Bloodsucker,” recast in a dark EBM mould. T.A.N.K. strikes back again with a solid, old-school EBM record that has been well crafted. Perhaps it could have been a bit harder overall for my taste, but otherwise, I have no complaints. (Rating:7½). Side-Line reported the announcement in April 2026, when Electro Aggression Records set “Broken Mirror” for release on May 30. Listen to “Zombie March”: Zombie March by T.A.N.K. About T.A.N.K. Reinhard Hüber, who came out of the 1990s German punk scene, launched T.A.N.K. in Dessau in 2001. The name stands for “Taktischer Angriff (auf’s) Nervenkostüm”. The first live appearance took place at the first Electric Tremor Festival in Dessau on 22 March 2002. The self-released “T.A.N.K.” EP landed in 2002, followed by the debut album “Musica Denaturale” on Ars Electrique in 2003. In 2011 the project contributed “Game of Men” to the 4CD set “Old School Electrology Volume One”. The second full-length, “Return”, came out in 2017 on Electric Tremor Dessau. Hüber also turned up in the Electro Aggression Records orbit through remix work connected to R010R and Synaptic Defect. “Broken Mirror” is the project’s third album and holds 19 tracks.
items._cn_summary: T.A.N.K.是德国老牌EBM项目，由Reinhard Hüber于2001年创立，历经九年才推出第三张专辑《Broken Mirror》，也是该厂牌在Electro Aggression Records的首发。专辑包含13首曲目加5首混音及1首翻唱，总计19轨。音乐以经典EBM配方为主：重型低音线搭配暗色弦乐编排，节奏强劲适合舞池，间或出现慢速段落展现氛围化质感。Hüber的人声粗粝扭曲，带有Dark Electro色彩。混音阵容包括Pyrroline、Sleepwalk等，Pyrroline的混音被特别赞许。对R010R《Bloodsucker》的黑暗EBM化翻唱是意外亮点。整体呈现扎实的复古取向，制作精良但创新性有限。

items.body: Arguably the defining metal band of their generation, Mastodon have never had a bad album, but their last four outings have been a significant step below the original classic four records that put them on the map. Beginning with the simultaneously simplified yet unfocused and maybe misguided The Hunter in 2011 and ending with the surprisingly successful and deeply personal, yet somehow forgettable double album Hushed and Grim (2021), the second chapter of Mastodon's career has been characterised by paradoxical inconsistencies. Although the band continued to push themselves with new concepts and textures, it also seemed like they'd fallen into something of a reliable holding pattern, emerging every few years to deliver something comfortingly yet never that excitingly Mastodon sounding. Marrow Deep, therefore, represents the beginning of a new chapter for Mastodon,* and presents an opportunity for the band to refresh and re-establish themselves, which they have taken to wholeheartedly. Whatever you think of the albums in between, it's hard to deny that Marrow Deep is the best Mastodon album since Once More 'round the Sun (2014)—or even longer, for (silly) people who don't like that album for whatever reason. The record continuously conjures up the Mastodonian triumphs of their past, with its overall sonic palette and songwriting sensibilities are something of a mix between what are perhaps the band's two greatest triumphs in Blood Mountain (2006) and Crack the Skye (2009). Even then though, it sounds less like a rehash or a missing link than something like what Emperor of Sand (2017) could and maybe should have been, in its masterful blend of classic and continuous Mastodon sounds.There are also a few new elements in play. Along with the added keyboards and emphasis on more traditional prog rock textures, "In the Ruins" represents something of a progressive metal Ouroboros, sounding like the sort of song Baroness have been ending their shows with since 2012, while "A Vampire's Demeanor" (featuring Lamb of God's Randy Blythe and Converge's Nate Newton) is an almost nu metal sounding song that joins Meshuggah's "Monstro-City" as perhaps one of the finest modern examples of the genre. This is also the first time Mastodon are working with Converge's Kurt Ballou and co-producer Patrik Berger, who is mostly known for co-writing Robyn's "Dancing on my Own" and a bunch of Charli XCX songs. Neither producer's trademark sound is really present though, with both combining instead into a perfect balance of metallic crunch and progressive clarity.Marrow Deep is, of course, the first Mastodon album without iconic founding guitarist Brent Hinds, who was ejected from the band last year, amid what appear to be increasingly troubling circumstances, before dying in a motorcycle accident a few months later. Hinds has since been replaced by Canadian guitarist Nick Johnston, whose work I am not familiar with, but who seems to be a good fit. In fact, Johnston does such a good job of fitting in that it's hard to really tell if he's there at all—whether he does such a good job of blending in with the rest of the band, or if he wasn't really that involved in the album's composition and is simply playing parts written with Hinds in mind. Conversely, Hinds' absence, while not necessarily damaging, is certainly noticeable. There are plenty of killer leads across the record, but none of them rip or ripple with the kind of fire he brought to the table. While he was certainly the least-accomplished of the three Mastodon vocalists, the absence of Hinds' distinctively garbled voice somewhat diminishes the album's dynamics, with Troy Sanders solidifying himself as the band's dedicated vocalist and Brann Dailor only really brought in as an added flavour here or there. You can hear the parts where Hinds' might have come in, and it makes you wonder what Marrow Deep might have been if he had continued on with the band instead.During this shake-up, Mastodon also took the opportunity to officially induct into their ranks Brazilian keyboardist João Nogueira, who has been collaborating with the band since 2021 and also plays in The Claypool Lennon Delirium. Unlike Johnston, Nogueira's contributions are immediately noticeable and largely elevating. Rather than dominating the album's atmosphere, his key sections are more often brought in as little flourishes during bridge and lead sections, that add such an exciting and distinctly "progressive" air to proceedings that it's a wonder Mastodon didn't introduce him or another keyboardist sooner. Unfortunately, while he might be a perfect sonic fit for the band, his personal associations raise some serious concerns. Outside of music, Nogueira has a longstanding association with conservative/right-wing, historical "revisionist" organisation Brasil Paralelo, where he goes by the name "Rasta" and hosts a sort of Daily Show-style comedy show. I don't speak Portuguese, so I can't comment on what he's actually saying in these videos, but—given Brasil Paralelo's associations with the rise of modern, neo-facisim, and their documented defenses and conspiracy theories about things like colonialism, slavery, sexism, homophobia and more—it's probably not good and certainly isn't being published somewhere that is. Hinds certainly had his own problems, but there's a big difference between personal gripes and uncoothness and being a mouthpiece for an institutionalised and (somewhat) influential right-wing conspiracy-spreading organisation. As far as I know, Mastodon have not addressed Nogueira's involvement with Brasil Paralelo in any interviews or other press material, and it is unclear whether they are aware of, or aware of the extent to which he serves as a spreader of their harmful, right-wing rhetoric, but I—and I'm sure many other Mastodon fans—are very interested to see how they respond once it is brought up.Additionally, for all its brilliant excesses, there's one other thing clearly missing from Marrow Deep, and that's big, fat, fuck-off riffs. The band's trademark, wiry guitar leads are on full display, and there are plenty of killer moments to be had throughout the songs—often simultaneously—but there's no "March of the Fire Ants", "Blood and Thunder", "High Road" or "Curl of the Burl" here, and hardly a "Wolf is Loose", "Oblivion", "Teardrinker" or "Sultan's Curse" either. Lead single "Your Ghost Again" is clearly the album's standout song, though that has far more to do with its luscious progressive layering and vocal melodies than the force of its six-string savagery. Opener "Barbarians Blood" lumbers rather than roars in, and while "Out like a Lamb" perhaps comes closest to becoming a classic Mastodon rocker, it's more in the "Spectrelight" style of anachronistic throwbacks than its own, definitive statement. Maybe its the lack of Hinds' contributions to its composition, but—as good as they all are—none of Marrow Deep's tracks announce themselves in the way the true Mastodon classics do.The other, arguably minor—but also rather unnecessary—weakness of Marrow Deep is its length. Mastodon have never been ones for short record lengths, with most of their outings sitting around the 50-minute mark. Considering the complexity of their compositions though, this length usually makes for a surprising and rewardingly concise experience, especially when it comes to something like Crack the Skye. At 65 minutes, Marrow Deep is easily Mastodon's longest, single-disc experience and you definitely feel it. What's more, the responsibility for this arguably bloated longevity lies squarely on superfluous final outing "The Three Fates." The album already had something of a false/elongated ending with "A Vampire's Demeanor," which provided a perfectly natural climax, before "The Vanishing" comes slinking in for one more round. Here, the encore presentation works perfectly, with the very "Planet Caravan"-sounding track —which features the actual Black Sabbath's Geezer Butler, alongside Gojira's Joe Duplantier—adding a natural and fitting epilogue to proceedings, whose spaced-out sounds allow the listener time to "come down" and reflect on the journey they've just been on—only to have "Three Fates" come crashing in again and ruin the whole effect, only to awkwardly end on a random riff that comes out of nowhere and simply stops suddenly. The song itself isn't bad and worth it on its own just to hear Clutch's Neil Fallon carrying on like a mad preacher, but I'd definitely say its the weakest track on here though and not nearly as suitable for closing the record as the two tracks before it, and might have worked better earlier on in the album.** As is, however, it feels tacked on and an instance of over-egging the progressive pudding.Marrow Deep is an album that asks a lot of its listeners, as the last couple Mastodon albums have as well. Unlike its immediate predecessors though, Marrow Deep feels fresh and inspired, pushing forward once again when it felt like Mastodon had maybe run out of things to say. While it sounds distinctly like Mastodon, it also sounds like a band who are still hungry and aren't satisfied to rest on their laurels the way they arguably have been for a while now. Get a few more riffs in there, cut down on the length and sort out the whole keyboardist situation, and they might yet be capable of delivering another definitive classic. Marrow Deep by Mastodon *Take a shot every time someone writes that while reviewing this album.**Due to promo streaming's penchant for playing final tracks second when listening on mobile for some reason, I can confirm it does indeed work quite well as the second rather than final track.

items.body:
1970 (April 10th, 1970 – IBC Studios, London)

Negotiations were now underway between Sean Murphy and several labels including Deram, CBS and Harvest, the EMI sub-label that had distributed Volume Two in the UK and already had Kevin Ayers in its stable. “They are still not an attraction in the very top bracket, so it was a pleasant surprise to see major companies throwing in genuinely massive bids earlier this year when the group was looking for a recording deal,” Richard Williams revealed. Ultimately, Soft Machine signed with CBS, but Third was self-financed, taken partly from studio sessions, but also from live recordings (“Facelift”) and edits and loops of tapes made by Mike Ratledge and Hugh Hopper at the home of Bob Woolford, who had let them use his Brenell and Stellavox tape recorders. Such infringements of accepted professional practices were only possible because CBS, having acquired a finished album, were no longer in a position to force the band to comply with them.

The benefit for Soft Machine in terms of artistic freedom is easy to measure. But this has to be balanced against the fact that the production on Third is, to put it bluntly, an unmitigated disaster. IBC, at the time the studio of choice for such notorious perfectionists as The Who and the Bee Gees, are probably less to blame than the band themselves who, in spite of the issues with Volume Two, are again credited as sole producers. The sound suffers from almost constantly saturated low frequencies and extremely vague mediums, the drums are much too low in the mix, as if played behind a closed door; and the organ is deprived of much of its biting impact through overwhelming equalization. Unfortunately the 2007 remaster, while an improvement, fails to rectify this.

What is problematic is that, as well as making the album an uncomfortable listen, its sub-par production lessens the claim, widely held at the time of its release, that Third represented musical state-of-the-art. This claim was based on Soft Machine’s ability, unparalleled among their contemporaries, to draw from and amalgamate an exceptionally wide range of influences. Starting out as a rock band, and then gradually moving towards jazz to invent a uniquely personal, and absolutely valid, British answer to American fusion, Soft Machine went even further, incorporating the influence of Stockhausen’s avant-garde and Terry Riley’s repetitive minimalism. Third’s ‘total’ vision, encompassing the entire spectrum of known musical genres, placed Soft Machine at the forefront of musical “progress” in 1970. However, horizons have since expanded to such an extent, beyond the Western tradition in particular, that this concept of universality has aged considerably.

In his insightful review of Third for Actuel, Paul Alessandrini wrote of “music to really listen to, no longer aiming for a purely physical vibration, more interiorized. Soft Machine have re-thought their musical influences – Riley, Cecil Taylor, Coltrane – to really make them their own, abandoning their aesthetics of random explosion in favor of a much more thought-out approach.” There are still occasional reminders of these sonic excesses that, as Alessandrini noted, had now largely disappeared from their music. Mike Ratledge's lengthy solo introduction to “Facelift” almost sounds like an electric exorcism, as if to rid Soft Machine of what still remains of that violence in order to reinvent their music in a more controlled manner, setting formal perfection as their new objective.

Considered as a whole, Hugh Hopper's piece represents the last remnant of Soft Machine’s early days, when they still favored spirit over form - here found lacking in both sound quality and performance, with a few train wrecks along the way - and were intent on disregarding the accepted rules. “Facelift” includes free sections increasingly at odds with Ratledge’s preoccupation with structure – and while as a keyboard player, he still embodies the band’s more radical leanings, Ratledge’s own compositions reveal a much less iconoclastic temperament. Hopper described his own approach at the time as “halfway between” that of Dean, “whose thing is really total improvisation, without any structure, and on the other extreme, [that of Ratledge] who's into entirely formalized musical forms.

“Moon in June” completes Robert Wyatt’s donation to Soft Machine of the material originally intended for his first solo album in 1968. It is interesting to note that Wyatt does this at the exact point where Soft Machine had shed any remaining reference to pop in their live repertoire. Looking back, Wyatt was certainly justified in saying that his side of Third was “the last chance I had to use all the things we'd done without being a jazz band. I wanted to get twenty minutes of it down somewhere.” And since his colleagues, reluctant to act as mere accompanists, had made no secret of their lack of interest in his songs, he recorded most of “Moon in June” on his own, repeating the modus operandi of the 1968-69 demo. Hugh Hopper and Mike Ratledge’s participation is again limited to the organ solo halfway through (Hopper also plays a short melodic theme earlier in the piece). Elton Dean wasn’t asked to contribute anything – Wyatt’s unconvincing justification being that he “hadn’t yet worked out how to work on [his] stuff with the added wind instruments.”

As there was no mention of this breach of band discipline in the sleeve notes, only the most astute listeners noticed that the organ heard during the first ten minutes was a Hammond rather than Ratledge’s signature Lowrey, that the playing clearly wasn’t Ratledge’s, and that most of the ‘bass’ parts were played on an electric piano. When the truth was finally revealed, Wyatt gave contradictory versions of what had happened – in one interview claiming that Ratledge and Hopper had “refused to play [on “Moon in June”] and I had to play it all myself,” in another that he’d “almost had to force them to get them to play on it, which I thought was rather unfair as I’d done my best to get into the music they were writing.” Probably the most objective and believable of Wyatt’s rationales was that he was “terrified it’d be played wrong” if he didn’t perform it all himself.

To approach “Moon in June” as a ‘message’ song would misrepresent Wyatt’s more mundane intent, insofar as the phonetic qualities of the words often seem to matter more to him than their meaning. In other words, “Moon in June” is above all a musical composition, a suite of instrumental sections, some of which are adorned with melodies and lyrics, and others not. The singing accompanies the music rather than vice-versa. In this respect, outside of a possible rivalry with Elton Dean and Wyatt’s inability to sing while drumming, there was no theoretical incompatibility between Soft Machine’s move towards jazz and the continued presence of Wyatt’s voice (even if limited to the Echoplexed scat singing of his solitary interludes during the band’s concerts). Dispensing with vocals was the single most questionable move in Soft Machine’s entire musical evolution, not to mention one whose commercial consequences cannot be underestimated. In different circumstances, Hugh Hopper would surely have joined Wyatt in lobbying for having at least some vocals, but in addition to his increasingly strained personal relationship with Wyatt, Hopper had at this point completely lost interest in non-instrumental music. “I find that using the human voice means asserting limitations to your music right from the start”, he explained in 1972. “I am more interested in the sounds generated by instruments, or electronic devices, because the possibilities offered by songs are much more limited than when experimenting with sounds.”

Even if there was no future for singing in Soft Machine, “Moon in June” at least offers evidence that Robert Wyatt, in a voice-free context, could still be more than “a session drummer for an interesting new species of jazz groups,” as long as he contributed to the writing. When it came to extended pieces, he could stand comparison with Mike Ratledge, even though he lacked any comparable academic background. In addition to its constant melodic inspiration, “Moon in June” is very skillfully constructed (indeed, its instrumental architecture had remained intact since 1968), and confirms Wyatt’s seemingly innate talent for making a coherent whole out of ill-assorted musical ideas.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑记录了Soft Machine第三张专辑的历史背景与制作过程。在CBS厂牌给予创作自由的前提下，乐队自筹资金录制，结合了录音棚素材、现场演出片段以及成员在家用磁带机上制作的循环段落。音乐上，软机器从摇滚出发，逐步走向爵士融合，并融入Stockhausen的先锋派与Terry Riley的极简主义重复技法，试图在1970年构建一种涵盖全谱系的音乐愿景。评论同时指出专辑制作存在低频过载、中频模糊、鼓声被掩埋等问题，削弱了作品的整体冲击力。文章内容涉及商业谈判、制作细节与音乐批评，为理解这张跨越多种流派的实验作品提供了历史与美学视角。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items._cn_summary: 该合辑收录圣多美和普林西比1970至1980年代的Puxa音乐录音，展现葡萄牙语非洲岛屿独特的节奏遗产。Puxa本身是融合merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等多种元素形成的复合风格，承载着被殖民历史禁止却依然延续的舞蹈传统。乐评着重分析了多把吉他交织缠绕、人声与旋律框架呼应的编曲特点，并强调这些录音诞生于一个缺乏成熟录音工业的小岛国，因此现存唱片尤为珍贵。Pedro Lima领衔的乐队以闷哑吉他与架子鼓的对抗制造张力，Sangazuza等人作品则展示了贝斯与键盘退出后由鼓与吉他主导的迷幻律动。Africa Negra的曲目作为现场长时间即兴演奏的缩影被特别提及，整张合辑以15首曲目呈现出小国音乐场景如何在全球离散与殖民交流中形成独立声音。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)
items.label: Analog Africa
items._genre: Beninese funk / afrobeat / vodun / Congolese rumba / Cuban son
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了贝宁歌手兼巫毒实践者Antoine Dougbè与Orchestre Poly-Rythmo de Cotonou在1977至1982年间合作的作品。乐评聚焦于Dougbè独特的Cavacha节奏——这一节奏由鼓手Belobi Meridjo从火车节拍中提炼，后广泛传播至刚果流行乐中。专辑呈现出鲜明的时代音色特征：吉他带有塑料质感光泽，合成器开始出现，音乐根源仍深植于七十年代。Cavacha节奏的影响与古巴son的影响在曲目中交替显现，前几首古巴元素较为突出，合成器铺底与闪烁的吉他构成层次丰富的织体。Dougbè被誉为'恶魔首相'，他的录音生涯虽短暂，仅有三张专辑和少量单曲，但此合辑展现了极高的音乐密度与独特文化深度。Analog Africa作为专注非洲音乐的独立厂牌，长期致力于挖掘此类被国际忽视的非洲音乐档案，这张合辑延续了这一使命。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio
items.label: Taragot
items._cn_summary: 挪威Camilla Hole Trio的新专辑《Langs》在延续探索精神的同时，从前作《Eventyrferd》的科幻合成器风格回归更具大地气息的声音。乐团以高音萨克斯为核心，自然融入了爵士语汇，作品取材于挪威西部民间音乐，如开场曲"Springleik"即源自挪威西部的同名传统舞曲。乐手之间的角色分工模糊而流动，萨克斯、低音提琴与鼓的对话在即兴中不断重组，配合模块合成器与颤音琴的叠加音色，使传统旋律在爵士框架中获得新的演绎空间。专辑延续了乐团将挪威本土民间音乐与即兴爵士、实验音色相融合的探索路径，展现出北欧爵士乐团对本土传统的独特再诠释。

items._cn_summary: 这是意大利暗氛围音乐人Stiehl（Gabriele Panci）长期项目New Risen Throne的最新专辑，作为该项目自2011年以来的第四张正式发行。音乐延续了其标志性的冰冷、仪式化美学，以缓慢移动的持续音为核心骨架，辅以仪式性或军事化的打击节奏，并叠加大量难以辨识的人声层，营造出肃穆而压迫的氛围。整张作品延续了暗潮与工业电子交界地带的探索传统，适合追求阴郁、冥想式聆听体验的听众。然而目前可见的乐评内容较为简短，仅提供了项目背景与基本风格描述，尚未深入探讨具体的作曲技法、声音设计或与同类型作品的差异，因此对专辑艺术水准的完整评估仍有局限。

items.body: The bassline on the new Death By Love track was recorded in a hotel room on a North American tour. Królowa Świata, out digitally on 28 August 2026, is the first original song the Polish-American duo have written in Polish, and it carries a guest bass part from Mario Usai of Clan Of Xymox. The gothic, industrial and trip-hop mix Death By Love brought to their debut album “444” is here pushed towards trance-styled synth sequencing. Królowa Świata by Death by Love The release runs four tracks: “Królowa Świata” (3:44), a “Psychotribe Psychoqueen Remix” of it (3:45), “Forest” (3:53) and a “Psychorchestra Remix” of “Forest” (4:02). Inga Habiba wrote the lyrics and sings; Peter Guellard handled synths and electric guitar; Usai played bass. Guellard produced and mastered the track at his Psychotribe Studio in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. The cover picture is by Robert Laska. How Death By Love built ‘Królowa Świata’ on the road The title translates as “Queen of the World”. Habiba addresses the song’s second person to herself rather than to a listener, and describes the writing that way: “these words are the whispers of my own subconscious, trying to break through the defensive armor I had built around myself.” Guellard began work on the track while touring the North American East Coast as a tech for Clan Of Xymox, carrying a portable rig and building around vocal takes Habiba had sent him. He cut the first guitar pass on Ronny Moorings‘ Rickenbacker. Usai then came into his hotel room, listened, and recorded the bass for the whole song. Guellard finished the arrangement at home, pairing fresh vocals from Habiba with the synth sequences. On writing in Polish, he commented: “Poland is our homeland, after all, even though at this point I’ve lived in the US longer than I ever lived there.” The video sets a vampire story in a mansion and a ballroom. Guellard built it from AI-generated imagery that he then edited and reworked with additional visual effects, the same method the duo used on their 2025 video for “Krakowski Spleen”. The track is on Bandcamp, Spotify and YouTube. About Death By Love Death By Love is a Polish-American project built around Polish singer-songwriter Inga Habiba and Polish-born, US-based producer, multi-instrumentalist and remix artist Peter Guellard. Habiba began performing in her teens with the new wave band Nizam, then fronted Monev, Ahimsa and the Warsaw gothic rock group Lorien, and worked with the folk-ethnic ensemble Habiarjan and the electronic act NUN Electro alongside her solo project CallMe. Guellard came up through the Polish goth band Blitzkrieg and later worked in the US dark-electronic underground with MACE, The Electric Hellfire Club, Venus in Furs and Dichro. A remix commission for NUN Electro’s “Hide” led to the pair working together on Habiba’s CallMe material, which became Death By Love. The duo signed to Distortion Productions and opened their catalogue with the three-track single “Strong Inside” at the end of January 2025. A Polish-language cover of Maanam’s “Krakowski Spleen”, with a video assembled from AI-generated visuals, followed in March 2025. They also appeared on COP International’s 75-track wildfire relief compilation “Los Angeles – From The Ashes”. Habiba and Guellard met in Warsaw in October 2024 to record “Strong Inside” and “Temros”, and completed the rest of the album across a year of file exchange between Europe and the United States. The single “Sellenno”, whose video was shot inside the disused Heinz ketchup factory in Pittsburgh, preceded the eleven-track concept album “444”, issued on Distortion Productions on CD and digital in February 2026 with a video for “Cosmic Power”. In July 2026 the duo put out “In Unity” as a set of remixes in tribute to the Polish act Wieloryb. “Królowa Świata” is their first release since.
items._cn_summary: 波兰裔美国双人组Death By Love发行新单曲《Królowa Świata》（世界之后），收录四首曲目。这是他们首支以波兰语创作的原创新作，歌词由主唱Inga Habiba撰写，被描述为潜意识试图冲破自我防御机制的低语。制作人Peter Guellard在北美巡演途中于酒店房间完成编曲，使用便携设备围绕Habiba提前录制的人声展开制作，并在Ronny Moorings的Rickenbacker吉他上录制了首段吉他声部。Clan Of Xymox的贝斯手Mario Usai在酒店房间内即兴录制了整首贝斯线。音乐风格从首张专辑的歌特、工业、trip-hop混合进一步推向trance式的合成器序列结构。封面与MV均采用AI生成影像并经后期重制，画面设定在吸血鬼故事的庄园与舞厅场景。作品延续了两人在地下暗潮场景中的合作脉络。

items.body: Review by Squonk19 — The latest album from Martin Springett's musical project, The Gardening Club, is called The Insubstantial Pageant, takes you on a wonderful, cinematic journey through time and place. Once again, the Toronto-based, ex-pat, musician, illustrator and author has conjured up a conceptual, narrative-driven album full of musical diversity and range, alongside a roster of talented musicians, many of whom have collaborated with him on previous albums.Based on an idea from Martin, with lyrics developed by Steve Bennett, the story of The Insubstantial Pageant revolves around a young woman whose father left the family when she was young and disappeared (for years he was rumoured to have been a spy). She embarks on a world-wide journey of discovery, following various clues as she travels to many different countries and getting glimpses of this enigmatic, ghostly figure. The storyline allows the band to explore many different musical cultures as we follow her travels - creating a genre-spanning instrumental spread, along with an intriguing mystery plot, full of suspense. As Bennett perceptively states: "Imagine Grahame Greene, Eric Ambler and John Le Carre locked in a studio with Procol Harum and Steely Dan."Martin's vocals and guitar work has crafted the diverse musical landscape complementing Steve's evocative lyrics, along with producer, guitarist and keyboardist Kevin Laliberte and Norm Macpherson's expressive orchestrations. Supported by Drew Birston on bass, and Rosendo Leon Arocha (Chendy) on drums and percussion - the lovely soprano vocals of Danie Friesen take us through the emotional sweep of the storyline. The music is progressive in nature, but informed by a range of styles, including folk, jazz, classical and ethnic elements, together with the group's blend of instrumentation, poetic lyricism and the stunning visual artistry that Martin provides with the CD booklet artwork.Ariel's Song starts the album's narrative in dreamy and ethereal fashion with Danie's haunting operatic vocals, acoustic guitar lines and gentle percussion - very much the prologue to The Insubstantial Pageant, where the daughter's quest to find her long lost father begins. Martin's distinctive vocals, joined later by Danie, merge with the acoustic guitar-led, lush instrumentation and vocal harmonies, with the rhythmic tempo ebbing and flowing, creating a darkly magical atmosphere. The music continues in a similar vein with two ballads, The Grey Men and then Geneva '46, as our protagonist follows the trail through captivating Cold War imagery, as Martin and Kevin's guitar and keyboards intertwine over the undulating drums. The former has a languid, almost desolate feel, whilst the latter one gradually picks up the pace and musical depth, with nice atmospheric electric guitar lines, as we picture a mysterious scene that would not be out of place in the classic film like The Third Man.Diary of a Grey Man draws us deeper into the story as we look at the scraps of an old diary to decipher the path that the daughter's father took. Martin and Danie's vocals mingle dreamily, with avant-garde touches, over Drew's eloquent fretless bass and elegant orchestrated string effects. Valparaiso '52 continues our journey as the story switches to post-colonial Chile - full of shadowy intrigue. There is some beautiful Spanish guitar patterns and misty harmonies over a more urgent, danceable beat, and Martin's vocals seemingly enacting a police interrogation of a shady diplomat, out of step with the new world order. The chorus is one of the catchiest on the album and stays long in the memory: "Our city - our rules. Nobody takes us for fools." We continue on our travels with the late-night blues/jazz of Chicago (South Side Story) which develops into a more funky, Steely Dan-like slab of soft rock, which provides a refreshing contrast - especially with some well-judged guitar and brass-like soloing.After the engaging, mid-way interlude of The Insubstantial Pageant (Reprise), Looking For Lorca continues the travelogue as we reach Spain - with Kevin's providing some lyrical flamenco-like guitar over a swaying gypsy rhythm. The lyrics express a feeling that the long quest for answers is more hopeful. The Hispanic influence continues with the sprightly A Sea of Emptiness (Cuban Sunset) before we arrive in the hot, arid, timeless vistas of North Africa, with Marrakech '64, with the vibrant sounds of Moroccan souks joining the atmospheric soundscapes and images of cream linen suited strangers with a Panama hat trawling through the back streets of the ancient city. The closing dynamic guitar soloing, siren-like vocals and resonating bass, work particularly well. You can imagine how much enjoyment Martin and the band had in trying the different musical styles as the storyline moved around the globe.East Meets West (Berlin 1979) follows the trail to the shadowy world of people around the Berlin Wall, just like scenes from a classic John Le Carre novel - and the trail seems to be getting warmer. The music enhances the cinematic imagery yet again, complementing the lyrics rather than dominating them. Martin's vocals do remind me of Andy Tillison of The Tangent at times, as well. A Long Distance Call has melancholic strings as the journey approaches the end, with A Return to the Park having a wistful, lush, orchestrated ambience with Danie's soaring operatic voice, marking the end of the story on a quiet park bench. It's been a long and varied quest for the daughter, both geographically and internally, but there is a warming sense of closure as the last notes play out.Martin Springett has conjured up an introspective musical story as evocative as any of his famed illustrations with The Insubstantial Pageant, the latest album from his musical project, The Gardening Club. With a diverse, but suitably measured, musical palette of genres and styles complementing Steve Bennett's lyrics, we follow an engaging story of a daughter's quest for a long-lost father through the dark corners of the post-war world. Progressive in scope rather than prog rock in nature, there is much to savour in the layered synergy between the acoustic and electric guitars, keyboards, bass, drums and varied lead vocals and harmonies. It is a refreshingly singular album that would please any listeners who value lyrically driven albums with thoughtful, nuanced musical themes. An album whose overall theme would make a wonderful book or film ? but one that remains addictively captivating and cinematic in musical form. Dedicated to the late Canadian saxophonist Wayne Kozak, is this album Martin's most ambitious and successful work to date? Quite possibly?(From The Progressive Aspect)

items._cn_summary: 这是Martin Springett音乐项目的最新专辑，以概念叙事为核心，讲述一位年轻女性追寻失踪父亲的跨国旅程。专辑在音乐上横跨多种风格，融入古典、爵士、民谣及世界音乐元素，配合Danie Friesen的女高音演绎，营造出电影化的氛围。歌词由Steve Bennett撰写，叙事充满冷战间谍小说的悬疑色彩，乐评人引用'格雷厄姆·格林、安布勒与勒卡雷与普罗科哈鲁姆、斯蒂利·丹共处一室'来形容其气质。器乐编排层次丰富，吉他、键盘与管弦乐交织，Norm Macpherson的弦乐编配增添了戏剧张力。Martin本人还为CD内册提供了视觉艺术作品，与音乐形成多维度呼应。作为跨界前卫摇滚作品，它在叙事性和世界音乐融合上展现出一定野心，但对偏好实验性前卫、爵士即兴或暗潮电子的听众来说，整体风格仍偏向传统的艺术摇滚叙事框架。

items.body: Review by alainPP — Gandalf's Fist offers a genre-defying brand of conceptual progressive rock, characterized by a dreamlike atmosphere, operatic storytelling, and a distinctive rock sound."The Lamplighter Suite" revisits the opening of *The Clockwork Prologue*, delivering a solid fifteen minutes of eclectic prog rock. It encompasses neo-prog, heavy metal, and folk?the full spectrum of this unclassifiable band. This remastered piece features imposing transitions, a grandiloquent scope, and a majestic finale driven by pompous orchestration backing Keri's signature vocals.The subsequent sections are drawn from their benchmark album *The Clockwork Fable*; "Parts I-VIII" sees Melissa's vocals stepping into this hidden rock opera. The original album featured guests like Blaze Bayley and spanned over three hours, complete with heavy, crushing metal breaks?though here, we get a condensed fifteen-minute version.The "Parts IX-XIII" sequence features Arjen as a guest?acting more as narrator than singer, evoking the Ayreon sound?alongside Melissa's enchanting, sultry, angelic vocals. The mood shifts from medieval-folk gentleness to doom metal reminiscent of Black Sabbath. The finale is sweeter and remains wonderfully eclectic, continuing to transport the listener into a symphonic, Tolkien-esque world.The conclusion comes with the brief "Parts XIV-XV," featuring Luke on vocals and a solemn, excellent melody with Middle Eastern and Japanese influences.Gandalf's Fist celebrates its sprawling 2016 album by weaving together its sixteen musical chapters; it serves as a "fake" compilation that highlights this complete, uninterrupted, masterful, and admirable work. Excellent. (4.5)
items._genre: neo-prog / symphonic rock / folk metal / concept rock
items._cn_summary: Gandalf's Fist以《The Lamplighter Suite》重新编排了其宏大的概念专辑《The Clockwork Fable》，将原本逾三小时的十六章节浓缩为精选辑式呈现。作品横跨新前卫摇滚、重金属、民谣及中世纪风格，甚至融入中东与日本音乐元素，营造出托尔金式的奇幻世界氛围。制作上运用大量管弦乐编制与歌剧化叙事手法，嗓音从庄严到天使般空灵多变，段落间过渡宏大而戏剧化。乐评指出这是一张"伪合辑"，实质是对2016年原作的系统性梳理与致敬。整体编排野心十足，但更偏向传统前卫摇滚框架内的综合呈现，与用户偏好的实验性、爵士即兴、电子声响设计等方向交集有限。
